<<PAGE 1>>
Bench: 
Mr. Justice Md. Ali Reza 
 
Civil Revision No. 3927 of 2015 
With 
Civil Revision No. 1238 of 2008 
 
Dr. Ashraf Hussain being died his legal heirs: 
1(a) Shahana Begum and others 
         ......petitioners  
                              -Versus- 
Haji Asaduzzaman Bhuiyan and others  
                                              ......opposite parties  
       
Mr. Zulfiqur Ahmed, Advocate 
 
 
 
 
......for the petitioners 
 
Mr. Sherder Abul Hossain, Advocate 
 
 
 
 
......for opposite parties  
 
Heard on: 18.06.2026, 30.06.2026, 
21.07.2026, 25.08.2026 and 03.09.2026 
 
Judgment on: 14.09.2026 
 
 
 
Civil Revision Number 3927 of 2015 has been filed by 
the plaintiff of the original suit. On the other hand Civil 
Revision Number 1238 of 2008 has been filed by Defendant 1 
of the original suit. Both the revisions are being disposed of by 
this single judgment. 
The plaintiff filed Title Suit Number 169 of 1985 in the 
Court of the Subordinate Judge, Brahmanbaria on 24.11.1985 
seeking declaration of title and recovery of possession. 
The plaintiff's case in brief is that the suit land 
admittedly belonged to Sailo Bala and her son Jagadish 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
Chandra Roy. They sold the suit land to the plaintiff by a 
registered deed dated 25.02.1976 and delivered possession to 
him. Accordingly the plaintiff obtained possession of 2 
decimals of land by virtue of his purchase. After obtaining 
possession the plaintiff constructed a tin-shed house with 
fencing thereon and started a medicine business in the said 
house. 
On 07.01.1977 the defendants entered into the suit land 
and demolished the said house and dispossessed him. The 
plaintiff then filed a case before the Court of the Regional 
Martial Law Administrator. On 05.08.1977 the said authority 
directed the Circle Officer of Nasirnagar Police Station to 
restore possession of the suit land to the plaintiff. Accordingly 
on 25.08.1977 the Circle Officer restored possession of the 
suit property to the plaintiff with police assistance. 
The plaintiff thereafter erected another house thereon 
and resumed his medicine business. In that situation on 
22.09.1978 the defendants again demolished the plaintiff's 
house and dispossessed him. The plaintiff again approached 
the Deputy Regional Martial Law Administrator for 
restoration of possession. On 06.09.1982 the Martial Law 
authority directed the Circle Officer to restore possession to 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
the plaintiff. However as the defendants offered to settle the 
matter with the plaintiff the Circle Officer did not restore 
possession to him. 
The defendants disclosed that they purchased the suit 
land from Shailabala Poddar. While assuring the plaintiff that 
they would settle the matter amicably the defendants 
continued to harass him for a long time. On 10.10.1985 during 
the civil court vacation they started constructing a pucca 
building on the suit land. As the plaintiff could not approach 
the court in time he lodged a complaint with the Nasirnagar 
Police Station. Thereupon the Officer-in-Charge of the police 
station issued a notice under Section 154. The defendants 
ignored the said notice and continued the construction work. 
In such circumstances the plaintiff filed the suit against 
the defendants seeking declaration of title to the suit land and 
recovery of possession. 
Defendants 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a written 
statement. Their case in brief is that Shailabala was the owner 
of 4 decimals of land comprising the 2 decimals of the suit 
land and another 2 decimals of non-suit land. While she was in 
possession she decided to sell the said land to Defendants 1 
and 2 for taka 15,000/- (fifteen thousand). However as the 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
S.A. khatian of the suit property had been wrongly recorded it 
was agreed that steps would be taken to correct the said record 
before registration of the sale deed. In the meantime an 
agreement for sale was executed and possession of the suit 
land was delivered to the defendants. 
In accordance with the terms of the agreement 
Defendants 1 and 2 paid taka 10,000/- (ten thousand) to 
Shailabala on 09.11.1974. The plaintiff was fully aware of the 
said agreement for sale. Subsequently on 29.09.1976 S.A. 
Khatian Number 604 was prepared in the name of Shailabala. 
Thereafter on 04.10.1976 Shailabala and her son Jagadish 
executed the sale deed. The deed was registered in favour of 
the defendants on 19.10.1976. 
Thus after acquiring title to the property the defendants 
constructed a two-roofed tin-shed house and have been 
carrying on business with the knowledge of all concerned 
including the plaintiff to the exclusion of others. 
In the meantime the then Sub-Divisional Officer, 
Brahmanbaria issued an illegal notice dated 05.10.1978 upon 
Defendant 1 in Case Number 3 of 1978 directing the 
defendants to vacate the property purchased by them. 
Defendant 1 submitted a written objection against the said 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
notice. However after hearing the objection was rejected on 
02.11.1978. 
Against the said order defendant 1 preferred a 
Miscellaneous Appeal before the Commissioner. After hearing 
the appeal was allowed on 21.07.1979. The plaintiff preferred 
an appeal before the Land Administration Board against the 
said order. The Chairman of the Board upheld the earlier order 
on 10.03.1983. 
The plaintiff thereafter filed another suit being Title Suit 
Number 27 of 1978. The said suit was dismissed for want of 
prosecution. Subsequently on 09.10.1985 the plaintiff 
submitted an application to the Superintendent of Police, 
Brahmanbaria. An investigation was conducted and a non-FIR 
case was started. The said case was subsequently dismissed. 
The plaintiff has no title or possession in the suit 
property. The alleged kabala dated 25.02.1976 relied upon by 
the plaintiff is forged and fraudulent. The plaintiff has been 
harassing the defendants on various false pretexts. The suit is 
therefore liable to be dismissed. 
The trial Court framed four issues in the suit. The 
plaintiff examined seven witnesses in support of his case. The 
defendants also examined seven witnesses. Both parties 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
adduced documentary evidence in support of their respective 
cases. In addition the Advocate Commissioner was examined 
as a Court witness. 
Initially 
the 
Subordinate 
Judge, 
First 
Court, 
Brahmanbaria decreed the suit on 30.03.1995. Against the said 
judgment and decree defendants 1 and 2 preferred Title 
Appeal Number 73 of 1995. The Additional District Judge, 
Second Court, Brahmanbaria allowed the appeal by judgment 
and decree dated 12.10.1998. 
Against the said judgment and decree plaintiff filed Civil 
Revision Number 4893 of 1998. The High Court Division 
remanded the case to the Court below by its order dated 
03.07.2000. 
Thereafter the Joint District Judge, First Court, 
Brahmanbaria dismissed the suit by judgment and decree 
dated 24.11.2004. Against the said judgment and decree 
plaintiff preferred Title Appeal Number 15 of 2005. The 
Additional District Judge, Second Court, Brahmanbaria 
allowed the appeal by judgment and decree dated 29.08.2007. 
He set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and 
remanded the case to the Court below. 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
Against the said judgment and decree defendant 1 filed 
the present Civil Revision Number 1238 of 2008. The plaintiff 
also filed Civil Revision Number 3927 of 2015. Both these 
civil revisions are now before us for disposal. 
Learned Advocate Mr. Zulfiqur Ahmed appearing on 
behalf of the plaintiff submits that the Courts below 
committed error of law resulting in an error in such decree 
occasioning faiture of justice. He submits that the trial Court 
failed to consider that the plaintiff has proved his title and also 
his earlier possession followed by dispossession by a series of 
documentary and oral evidence. He further submits that both 
the Courts below failed to appreciate that plaintiff has made 
out a definite case of his specific possession in the suit land. 
Such possession is apparent from the materials on record. 
He submits that the appellate Court remanded the suit on 
the ground of want of specification. Such ground is not tenable 
in law. He further submits that law permits a co-sharer who 
has been enjoying specific possession of a specified portion of 
land to recover possession of that portion if dispossessed. 
Such recovery is permissible under Article 142 of the 
Limitation Act. 

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8
He also submits that the plaintiff's document is earlier in 
point of time. According to Section 47 of the Registration Act 
the date of registration determines the operation of the 
registered document. The execution of the bainapatra is 
therefore not an issue which requires consideration and 
decision in the present case. In this regard he refers to the case 
of Zamir Uddin Ahmed Vs. Ziaul Haq and others reported in 
49 DLR 622. 
He finally submits that the order of remand is 
unnecessary. There is sufficient evidence on record to decide 
the suit on merit. He therefore prays that the suit may be 
decreed in revision. 
On the other hand learned Advocate Mr. Sherder Abul 
Hossain appearing on behalf of the defendant submits that the 
trial Court correctly dismissed the suit upon proper 
appreciation of the evidence. The appellate Court however 
upon misreading and non-consideration of material evidence 
wrongly remanded the suit by setting aside the decree passed 
by the trial Court. Thus the appellate Court committed error of 
law occasioning failure of justice. 
He submits that long before the alleged purchase of the 
land by the plaintiff the defendants entered into an agreement 

<<PAGE 9>>
 
9
for sale with Sailobala. Pursuant thereto the sale deed in 
favour of the defendants was executed and registered. The 
defendants obtained possession of the suit land. The plaintiff's 
case of earlier possession followed by dispossession is 
therefore completely false. 
He further submits that the plaintiff had full knowledge 
of the earlier agreement for sale. His subsequent document is 
forged and fraudulent. The trial Court rightly dismissed the 
suit. The appellate Court wrongly remanded the suit as a 
matter of course although sufficient evidence was available on 
record. 
He also submits that the land claimed by the plaintiff is 
not sufficiently specified. Therefore the present suit for 
recovery of possession cannot be decreed in view of Order 7 
Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He finally submits that 
the suit is false and is liable to be dismissed. 
I have heard the learned Advocates for both sides and 
perused the materials on record and gone through the 
judgments passed by the Courts below. I have also noticed that 
the rule issuing orders challenge the judgments and orders of 
the Courts below. However the decrees have not been 

<<PAGE 10>>
 
10
specifically challenged although the decree of the trial Court 
has been filed with the two civil revisions. 
Since sufficient evidence is available on record I am of 
the view that justice will be best served if the suit is decided 
on merit on the basis of the evidence already on record rather 
than sending it down on remand to either of the courts below. 
The suit has been pending since 1985. In the circumstances I 
propose to decide the suit on merit without any further 
remand. 
It is on record that the instant suit was decreed earlier on 
30.03.1995. Against the said judgment and decree the 
defendants preferred Title Appeal Number 73 of 1995 which 
was allowed. The plaintiff then preferred Civil Revision 
Number 4893 of 1998. In that revision the suit was sent down 
on remand. Thereafter the trial Court dismissed the suit on 
24.11.2004. Against the said judgment and decree the plaintiff 
preferred Title Appeal Number 15 of 2005. In that appeal the 
judgment and decree of the Court below was set aside and the 
suit was sent down on remand on 29.08.2007. 
It appears from Exhibit-1 which is an admitted document 
that C.S. Khatian Number 59 contains 9 decimals of land in 
Plot Number 137/701. The suit property was subsequently 

<<PAGE 11>>
 
11
inherited by Shailabala Roy and her son Jagadish Chandra 
Roy as successive heirs of the C.S. recorded tenant. It is also 
admitted by both parties that although the S.A. khatian was 
wrongly prepared the record was subsequently corrected in the 
name of Shailabala by an order dated 29.09.1976 passed in the 
record correction case. 
The plaintiff's case is that while Shailabata and her son 
were in possession of the suit land as owners they sold the 
same to the plaintiff by a deed executed and registered on 
25.02.1976 and delivered possession to him. After purchasing 
the land the plaintiff constructed a tin-shed house thereon and 
started medicine business. The plaintiff produced the original 
sale deed dated 25.02.1976 before the Court. The same was 
marked as Exhibit-2. 
P.W. 1 in his deposition stated that after Shailabala sold 
the suit property to him by a registered deed he constructed a 
one-roofed house with a door and started medicine business 
therein. On 07.01.1977 the defendants demolished the house 
and dispossessed him. He then filed a case before the Martial 
Law Court. Thereafter the Circle Officer was directed to 
restore possession to him by Exhibits 4 and 4(ka). In 

<<PAGE 12>>
 
12
accordance 
with 
Exhibit-4(kha) 
dated 
25.08.1977 
he 
recovered possession of the suit property. 
After resuming his business the defendants again 
demolished his house and dispossessed him on 22.09.1978. He 
again obtained an order for restoration of possession from the 
Martial Law Court. However the defendants offered to settle 
the matter amicably. Without settling the matter they started 
constructing a pucca building on the suit land on 10.10.1985. 
In cross-examination P.W. 1 stated that Shailabala was 
the owner of 4 decimals of land including the suit land. He 
also specifically described the boundaries of the suit property 
as stated in his deed. He stated that the land to the north of the 
suit property belonged to Dudumia and others and was 
subsequently possessed by Isab Ali. The land to the south 
belonged to Wajuddin. The land to the east belonged to the 
vendor Shailabala herself. The Land to the west belonged to 
Wajuddin and was subsequently possessed by Ahmad Ali and 
others. 
P.W. 2 in his deposition stated that he constructed the 
plaintiff's house on the suit land and P.W. 3 was also present 
there. He stated that the plaintiff practised medicine in that 
house. He further stated that he constructed the house twice. In 

<<PAGE 13>>
 
13
cross-examination he clearly stated that the first house was a 
tin-shed house and the second one was made of bamboo. 
P.W. 3 also gave similar evidence. He stated that the 
house was subsequently constructed with bamboo and the 
plaintiff practised medicine there. In cross-examination P.W. 3 
stated that he heard from the market watchman that the 
plaintiff's house was demolished. The said watchman was 
examined as P.W. 4. 
P.W. 4 in his deposition stated that there was a tin-shed 
house on the suit land. He was the market watchman. He 
stated that the defendants demolished the said house and he 
informed the doctor about the incident. He further stated that 
the defendants demolished the house again on the second 
occasion. In cross-examination he stated that the defendants 
has been in possession of the suit land for 16 or 17 years. 
P.W. 6 supported the boundaries given by P.W. 1. He 
stated that he was the owner of 2 decimals of land adjoining 
the suit property on the west. He further stated that before he 
acquired title Wajuddin was the owner in possession of his 
land. 

<<PAGE 14>>
 
14
P.W. 7 also gave evidence in support of P.W. 1 and P.W. 
6 and described the boundaries of the suit land in similar 
terms. 
It does not appear that the defendants could elicit any 
material contradiction from any of the witnesses of the 
plaintiff in cross-examination. The evidence of the plaintiff's 
witnesses regarding his earlier possession and subsequent 
dispossession therefore remains substantially unshaken. 
P.W. 5 is the deed writer. He stated in his deposition that 
he wrote the deed on 25.02.1977 and the transaction took 
place in his presence. It also appears from his cross-
examination that he is the identifier of the said deed. The deed 
itself supports this fact. 
In the written statement the defendants did not 
specifically deny the documents produced by the plaintiff as 
Exhibits 4 series and 5 series. They also failed to elicit any 
material contradiction from the plaintiff's witnesses in respect 
of his earlier possession and subsequent dispossession. 
The deed writer of Exhibit-2 identified the executants in 
accordance with Rule 46 of the Registration Rules. The 
plaintiff also produced the original deed before the court. 

<<PAGE 15>>
 
15
Thus on a consideration of the documentary and oral 
evidence discussed above it is proved according to law that the 
plaintiff obtained possession of the suit land by virtue of 
Exhibit-2 and was subsequently dispossessed therefrom. 
On the other hand D.W. 1 stated in his deposition that 
Shailabala sold the suit property to the defendants on 
09.11.1976 upon receiving taka 10,000/- (ten thousand) out of 
the agreed consideration of taka 15,000/- (fifteen thousand) 
and delivered possession to them. He further stated that after 
obtaining possession the defendants have been carrying on 
business thereon. However he admitted that he did not know 
the exact area of the suit land. He also did not know which 
part of the plot comprised the suit land. 
In cross-examination when questioned about the 
agreement for sale D.W. 1 stated that he has not produced the 
said agreement before the Court. 
D.W. 2 stated in his deposition that he is a witness to the 
agreement for sale and his signature was marked as Exhibit-
Ka. In cross-examination he admitted that the ink used for 
writing the agreement and the ink used for his signature are 
different. 

<<PAGE 16>>
 
16
D.W. 3 gave evidence regarding the title and possession 
of the defendants over the suit land. In cross-examination he 
stated that he is the brother-in-law of the defendant. 
D.W. 4 Gour Das Deb deposed as the deed writer of the 
agreement for sale. In cross-examination he admitted that no 
licence number was mentioned in the agreement. 
D.W. 5 and D.W. 6 gave evidence regarding the 
possession of the defendants. D.W. 7 deposed as a witness to 
the deed executed by the defendants on 04.10.1976. 
The unregistered baina patra was first brought before the 
Court on 15.02.1995. On that date the witness to the baina 
patra proved his signature which was marked as Exhibit-Ka. 
However the baina patra itself was not exhibited on that date. 
Subsequently D.W. 4 produced the baina patra before the 
Court on 17.11.2003 and it was marked as Exhibit-Gha. 
Perusal of Exhibit-Gha discloses three important matters. 
First the ink used for writing the baina patra is different from 
the ink used for the signatures of the witnesses. Secondly two 
round seals of the Court of the Second Subordinate Judge, 
Comilla appear on the upper portion of both pages of the baina 
patra. The date appearing on those seals is 23.08.1971. 
However the alleged baina patra was executed in 1974 and the 

<<PAGE 17>>
 
17
stamp paper was also purchased in 1974. Thirdly the baina 
patra was executed on 09.11.1974. But the stamp paper was 
purchased on 28.10.1974 by a person whose identity and 
connection with the baina patra have not been explained by 
the defendants. The agreement appears to have been 
subsequently created and fabricated and cannot be treated as 
genuine.  
D.W. 7 produced the deed of the defendants before the 
Court on 13.03.2004 and the same was not tendered in 
evidence by the transferees of the document and no 
explanation has been offered to that effect. The deed was 
executed on 04.10.1976 and was marked as Exhibit-Uma. 
Exhibit-Uma also contains several suspicious features. In 
Exhibit-Uma the seals appearing from the reverse side of the 
first page up to the last page of the affidavit are in black ink 
which is contrary to Rule 45(2) of the Registration Rules.  
It is also significant that the recital of Exhibit-Uma 
contains no reference to the alleged baina patra dated 
09.11.1974. The defendants claim that the plaintiff purchased 
the land with knowledge of the baina patra. If that claim were 
true there should have been some reference to the baina patra 

<<PAGE 18>>
 
18
in the deed of the defendants. No such reference is found in 
Exhibit-Uma. 
Moreover although Exhibit-Uma was executed on 
04.10.1976 the stamp paper is shown to have been purchased 
on 07.07.1976. The stamp paper was not purchased by either 
the executant or the recipient of the deed. No satisfactory 
explanation has been given for this circumstance. There are 
also inconsistencies in the signatures given by the Sub-
Registrar. 
Thus the 1971 seals appearing on Exhibit-Gha and the 
inconsistencies apparent in Exhibit-Uma create serious doubt 
about the genuineness of both documents. Having considered 
the surrounding circumstances and the evidence of the 
defendants I find that the alleged baina patra and the 
subsequent deed were not prepared and executed in the 
ordinary course to the satisfaction of the Court. They were 
created for the purpose of supporting the false claim of the 
defendants. 
A question has also been raised regarding the boundaries 
of the suit land. The Courts below failed to notice that the 
plaintiff clearly proved the boundaries of the suit land through 
his pleadings and evidence. The Commission Report dated 

<<PAGE 19>>
 
19
07.09.1986 and the case map forming part of the record show 
that the suit land has been specifically shown in light orange 
colour in the map. The Commissioner gave evidence as C.W. 
1 on 01.12.1988. The defendants could not show any material 
inconsistency in his evidence through cross-examination. 
Thereafter upon hearing on the Commission Report on 
11.04.1990 the Court kept the report on record. 
The objection raised by the learned Advocate for the 
defendants regarding the alleged uncertainty of the boundaries 
is without substance. The use of one or two complex sentences 
in the plaint in describing the boundaries does not make the 
suit land uncertain. The plaintiff clearly described and proved 
the identity of the suit land through the schedule to the plaint, 
the schedule to Exhibit-2 and the evidence of P.W. 1, P.W. 6 
and P.W. 7 along with Exhibit-5 dated 16.10.1985 and 
Exhibit-5(Ka) dated 28.10.1985. The Commission Report and 
the case map further support that description. Plaintiff has 
complied with the provision of Order 7 Rule 3 of the Code of 
Civil Procedure to the satisfaction of the Court. 
At one stage of the hearing the learned Advocate for the 
plaintiff brought to the notice of the Court the certified copy of 
B.S. Khatian Number 579 issued on 25.06.2025. It appears 

<<PAGE 20>>
 
20
from the said khatian that the suit land has been recorded in 
the name of the plaintiff. The names of the defendants have 
been mentioned in the remarks column as persons in forcible 
possession. The said B.S. Khatian is a finally published 
record-of-rights under Section 144A of the State Acquisition 
and Tenancy Act. When supported by other evidence such a 
record carries strong presumptive value. It is also a public 
document within the meaning of Section 74(1)(iii) of the 
Evidence Act. The Court may take notice of it in the interest 
of justice even if it has not been formally proved in evidence. 
The certified copy appears to have been issued under Section 
76 of the Evidence Act from the record room of the Deputy 
Collector, Brahmanbaria. It bears the relevant signatures and 
endorsements of the concerned officers. It was prepared by the 
office assistant and verified by the record-room verifier. It was 
also examined and certified as correct by the record keeper. 
Upon consideration of the entire evidence and the 
surrounding circumstances it appears that the plaintiff was 
dispossessed from the suit land in 1978 and has been seeking 
justice since then. P.W. 4 in his cross-examination on 
25.09.1994 stated that the defendants has been in possession 
for about sixteen or seventeen years. His evidence thus 

<<PAGE 21>>
 
21
supports the plaintiff's case that he was dispossessed from the 
suit land in or about 1978. 
The evidence adduced in support of defence is not 
reliable. The alleged baina patra and the subsequent deed are 
surrounded by suspicious circumstances and have been found 
to be fabricated and fraudulent. 
The submission based on Section 47 of the Registration 
Act does not assist the defendants. The defendants cannot 
claim priority over the plaintiff's earlier registered deed merely 
by relying upon an alleged earlier unregistered baina patra. 
The title claimed by the defendants cannot be treated as 
relating back to the date of the alleged baina patra. In the facts 
of the present case the earlier registered deed of the plaintiff 
must prevail over the subsequent deed relied upon by the 
defendants. 
In the present case the plaintiff has clearly proved his 
title as well as his earlier possession and subsequent 
dispossession by competent evidence.  
In view of the above discussion the judgments and 
decrees passed by the Courts below are set aside. The Rule 
issued in Civil Revision Number 3927 of 2015 is made 

<<PAGE 22>>
 
22
absolute. The Rule issued in Civil Revision Number 1238 of 
2008 is discharged. 
The plaintiff is entitled to a decree for declaration of title 
to the suit property and for recovery of possession thereof. 
Defendants 1 and 2 are directed to remove all obstructions 
from the suit land and to hand over possession of the same to 
the plaintiff within 30(thirty) days from the date of 
communication of this judgment and order. In default the 
plaintiff shall be entitled to recover possession through the 
process of the Court. 
Let a copy of this judgment be communicated to the 
Courts below forthwith and the Lower Courts' Records be sent 
down at once. 
 
Md. Ali Reza, J: 
 
 
 
  
 
 
 
Naher-B.O
input_summary: The REVISIONIST, the original plaintiff, challenged the appellate court's order dated 29 August 2007 concerning remand of a land title and possession suit against the OPPOSITE PARTIES. The REVISIONIST sought a declaration of title and recovery of the land, arguing that an earlier registered purchase, specific possession and later dispossession were established and that further remand was unnecessary. The OPPOSITE PARTIES relied on an earlier sale agreement and a later deed, disputed the REVISIONIST's documents and argued that the land was inadequately identified. The parties referred to the Limitation Act, the Registration Act and the Code of Civil Procedure.
explanation: UNCERTAIN: The court relied on several legal provisions, while its decision principally rested on factual findings rather than one clearly decisive statute. It found the REVISIONIST's registered deed and substantially consistent witness testimony established title, previous possession and subsequent dispossession. The competing agreement and deed had suspicious seals, inconsistent details and other features indicating fabrication. The pleadings, witnesses, commission report and map sufficiently identified the property under Order VII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The court also considered the record of rights and found enough evidence to determine the suit without another remand. In the connected revisions, the plaintiff REVISIONIST obtained relief, while the defendant REVISIONIST did not.

This appeal was directed against the judgment and order of 
conviction and sentence dated 25.03.2024 passed by the learned 
Divisional Special Judge, Dhaka in Special Case No. 48 of  2022 
arising  out of Joydebpur Model Police Station Case No. 96 dated 
27.01.2024 under Sections 467/468/471/420 of the Penal Code 
convicting the appellant under Sections 467/468/471/420 of the

2 
 
Penal Code and sentencing him to suffer rigorous imprisonment 
for 04 (four) years and to pay a fine of Tk. 20,000/- (twenty 
thousand) in default to suffer further 03 (three) months of simple 
imprisonment more and also convicted another co-accused of this 
instant case. 
The prosecution case in brief is that one Mollah Mahfuz Al 
Hossain, 
Registrar 
(Additional 
Responsibilities), 
National 
University, Gazipur as informant lodged a First Information 
Report (FIR) with the Joydebpur Police Station, Gazipur against 
the convict-appellant and others under Sections 467/468/471/420 
of the Penal Code alleging inter alia that the appellant is a lower 
assistant joined on 19.12.1999 in National University, Gazipur 
and took salary from 11 years. The committee, compromises with 
5 members after concluded the inquiry found that his Degree 
(pass) Certificate was fake. After asking information regarding the 
certificate from the registrar of the National University, the 
hearing committee also confirmed that the alleged certificate was 
not issued in the name of this appellant rather only using similar 
name, the appellant somehow obtained alleged certificate from the 
certificate Section of the National University and the committee 

<<PAGE 3>>
3 
 
also found allegation against other co-accused of this instant case 
and hence the case. 
After investigation the investigating officer submitted 
charge sheet being No. 1381 dated 20.11.2016 against the 
appellant under Sections 467/468/471/420 of the Penal Code, 
1860 with Sections 5(2) of the Anti-Corruption Prevention Act, 
1947. Thereafter, the case has been transferred to the learned 
Divisional Special Judge, Dhaka for trial, which as renumbered as 
Special Case No. 48 of 2022. After hearing the learned trial court 
delivered judgment on 25.03.2024 and convicting the appellant 
under sections 467/468/471/420 of the Penal Code and sentencing 
him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for a period of 04(four) years 
and a fine of tk. 20,000/-(twenty thousand) in default of payment 
of fine to suffer further 03(three) months of simple imprisonment 
and also convicted another co-accused of this instant case. 
Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the judgment and 
order dated 25.03.2024 the convict-appellant preferred this appeal.  
On 21.10.2024 the convict-appellant enlarged on bail by 
this Hon’ble court in Criminal Appeal No. 8058 of 2024 for a 

<<PAGE 4>>
4 
 
period of 1(one) year. Lastly, the bail was extended for till 
disposal of this appeal on 21.10.2025. The Lower Court Records 
(L.C.R) was attached with this appeal on 26.08.2025.  
The prosecution examined as many as 12(twelve) witnesses 
in support of their case but on behalf of the defense no one 
examined.  
Mr. Mohammad Ali, learned Advocate with Mr. Md. 
Mahbubur Rahman with Mr. Md. Amzad Hossain Riyad, learned 
Advocates appearing on behalf of the convict-appellant while Mr. 
M. Sarwar Hossain, learned advocate appeared for the Anti

input_summary: The APPELLANT challenged the special judge's judgment dated 25 March 2024 concerning convictions for forgery, use of a forged document and cheating, and sought relief from the convictions and sentence. The STATE and a RESPONDENT opposed the appeal. The prosecution alleged that the APPELLANT used another person's degree certificate to obtain employment and promotion. The APPELLANT argued that the original certificate was not produced, that a degree was unnecessary under the applicable service rules, and that departmental findings did not establish criminal guilt. The RESPONDENT pointed to evidence of a requested change to the father's name. The parties referred to the Penal Code and the Evidence Act.
explanation: UNCERTAIN: The court referred to service rules and the absence of the original certificate but did not clearly identify an Act as the basis of its decision; the Evidence Act provisions were presented as the APPELLANT's argument. The court noted that the applicable service rules did not require a degree for the APPELLANT's appointment or promotion. It also observed that the certificate reproduced in the record had no space for a father's name and questioned how the authority established a discrepancy in that name when the original certificate had not been produced before the trial court.

The prosecution case, in brief, is that Md. Amber Ali, Post 
Office Inspector, Lalmonirhat Sub-Division, lodged a written

Additional Duty Upazila Post Master, Aditmari Upazila Post

entrusted with the government money, had dishonestly 
misappropriated the said amount and absconded. On such 
allegation, Aditmari Police Station Case No. 17 dated 12.01.2011 
was instituted against him under section 409 of the Penal Code 
and section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. 
 
After investigation submitted charge sheet being No. 148 
on 15.12.2011 under section 409 of the Penal Code read with 
section 5(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1947 against the 
appellant.   
 
The learned Special Judge, Lalmonirhat  accepted the 
police report transferred the record to the Sessions Judge for trial 
and renumbered as Special Case No. 02 of 2012 and sent the 
record to the Special Judge, Lalmonirhat. 
 
The learned Special Judge, Lalmonirhat framed charge 
against the appellant. On 23.10.2014 the learned trial court 
passed the judgment convicting the appellant under Section 409 
of the Penal Code read with Section 5(2) of the Anti-Corruption 
Act, 1947.

4

23.10.2014 the appellant filed this appeal before this Court.  
The prosecution as many as 12 prosecution witnesses 
produced before the trial for prove the case.

allegations in the FIR, the prosecution must prove beyond 
reasonable doubt not only the existence of the alleged shortage, 
but also that the money was entrusted to, dominion of, the 
accused by virtue of his official capacity and that he dishonestly 
misappropriated or converted the same to his own use, thereby 
committing criminal breach of trust under section 409 of the 
Penal Code. The prosecution must also establish the requisite 
ingredients of the offence under section 5(2) of the Prevention of 
Corruption Act, 1947. The crucial question, therefore, is whether 
the evidence on record establishes a clear and reliable nexus 
between the alleged shortage and the accused's dishonest 
misappropriation or conversion of the money. 
For the purpose of disposing of the appeal, I shall now 
examine the evidence on record. 
P.W.1, Md. Ambar Ali, Post Office Inspector, Lalmonirhat 
District, in his examination-in-chief, stated that on 12.01.2011 he

duties of Upazila Post Master from 24.10.2010 to 11.01.2011.

Faruk replied that he would do so the following morning. At 
about 2:00 p.m, Omar Faruk left the office for lunch but did not 
return during office hours. Ekramul Haque thereafter informed 
the Post Master, Lalmonirhat, over telephone and reported the 
matter to the authorities. P.W.1, subsequently went to the 
Aditmari Upazila Post Office and, finding Omar Faruk absent, 
informed the UNO. At about 10:00 p.m, DPMG, Rangpur, Abul

Hossain, Noor Nabi and other officers and employees, arrived at 
the post office. The UNO and the Officer-in-Charge of Aditmari

and other articles was prepared. It revealed a shortage of Tk. 
13,12,750.94, although Tk.52,526/- in cash and stamps and

his absence. These circumstances, without proof of dishonest

prove the case beyond all reasonable doubt.

place on different two dates e.i. 14.06.2011 and 29.09.2011 and

said post office. Hence, it appears on the face of the record that 
the appellant was responsible for the alleged misappropriation of 
the funds in question.  
Heard the learned advocates for the respective parties and 
perused the documents on record. 
Having considered the evidence of P.Ws. 1-12 and the 
documents exhibited by the prosecution, I find that the 
prosecution has been able to establish the existence of a shortage 
of postal money amounting to Tk. 13,12,750.94 at Aditmari 
Upazila Post Office after the accused left the office without 
handing over charge. P.Ws.1, 2, 8 and 9 support the preparation 
of the inventory and the detection of the shortage. P.Ws.4 and 5 
stated that the accused received Tk.9,00,000/- from the 
Lalmonirhat Head Post Office on 09.01.2011, while P.W.3 stated 
that Tk.3,00,000/- was deposited at the Aditmari Post Office. 

<<PAGE 19>>
19 
 
The remaining witnesses are mainly formal, procedural or 
investigating witnesses. 
The crucial question, however, is not merely whether there 
was a shortage, but whether the prosecution has proved beyond 
reasonable doubt that the alleged missing money was entrusted 
to, or was within the dominion of, the accused in his capacity as 
a public servant and that he dishonestly misappropriated or 
converted the same to his own use. 
On this material point, the prosecution evidence falls short 
of the required standard. None of the witnesses saw the accused 
taking, retaining, converting or misappropriating the alleged 
missing money. Although P.Ws.4 and 5 stated that the accused 
received Tk.9,00,000/- from the Lalmonirhat Head Post Office, 
the prosecution failed to establish its subsequent delivery to or 
receipt at Aditmari Post Office. Significantly, P.W. 12, the 
Investigating Officer, admitted that there was no specific entry 
showing receipt of the said amount at Aditmari Post Office, no 
document evidencing its dispatch, and that he could not say 
whether the money had actually been paid. Thus, the evidence 
regarding receipt of Tk.9,00,000/- does not, by itself, establish 
that the amount came into the possession or dominion of the 

<<PAGE 20>>
20 
 
accused at Aditmari Post Office and was thereafter dishonestly 
misappropriated by him. 
Likewise, although P.W.3 proved the recording of 
Tk.3,00,000/- in his deposit book, his evidence does not establish 
that the accused personally received or appropriated the said 
amount. The mere existence of a transaction, followed by a 
subsequent shortage, cannot dispense with proof of the accused's 
possession or dominion over the particular money and his 
dishonest conversion thereof. 
The evidence further discloses material deficiencies 
concerning the authorized cash balance, the mode of remittance, 
requisitions, authorizations and the custody and movement of the 
alleged missing cash. P.W.1 admitted that he did not furnish the 
Memo of Authorized Balance. P. Ws.4 and 5 also referred to 
procedural restrictions concerning the transmission of substantial 
amounts of cash. P.W.11 failed to establish the alleged seizure of 
incriminating articles, while the evidence of P.W.12, though 
relevant to the investigation and seizure of documents, does not 
provide substantive proof of the actual misappropriation. 
Mere proof of shortage or loss of public money does not, 
by itself, establish criminal breach of trust. The prosecution must 
independently prove the foundational fact of entrustment or 

<<PAGE 21>>
21 
 
dominion and thereafter establish dishonest misappropriation or 
conversion by the accused. In the present case, the evidence, 
taken at its highest, establishes a shortage and raises suspicion 
against the accused, particularly because he left the office 
without handing over charge. Suspicion, however strong, cannot 
take the place of proof. 
The fact that the accused was absent from the office, failed 
to hand over charge, or was found to have been associated with 
the handling of postal money may constitute circumstances 
requiring explanation, but such circumstances cannot, in the 
absence of reliable evidence connecting him with the particular 
missing amount, establish the essential ingredients of the 
offence. The prosecution was required to bridge the evidentiary 
gap between the existence of the shortage and the accused's 
dishonest appropriation of the money. That essential link is 
absent in the present case. 
Accordingly, I find that the prosecution has failed to prove 
beyond reasonable doubt that the alleged missing amount was 
entrusted to, or was within the dominion of the accused and that 
he dishonestly misappropriated or converted the same to his own 
use. Consequently, the essential ingredients of Section 409 of the 
Penal Code and Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption 

<<PAGE 22>>
22 
 
Act, 1947, have not been established by substantive and reliable 
evidence. 
In view of the foregoing discussion, I am of the considered 
view that the prosecution has failed to prove the charge against 
the accused beyond reasonable doubt. The finding of guilt 
recorded by the learned trial Court is therefore not sustainable in 
law. 
In the result, the appeal is allowed and the impugned 
judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 23.10.2014, 
passed by the learned Special Judge, Lalmonirhat, in Special 
Case No. 02 of 2012 is hereby set aside. Consequently, the 
accused, Md. Omar Faruk, is acquitted of the charges. The bail 
bond stands discharged. 
The Lower Court Records be sent down at once. 
Let a copy of this judgment be communicated to the Court 
below forthwith. 
 
 
 
 
 
Shokat (B.O.)
input_summary: The APPELLANT challenged the special judge's judgment dated 23 October 2014 concerning convictions and sentences for alleged misappropriation of postal funds, and sought relief from them. The STATE and a RESPONDENT opposed the appeal. The prosecution alleged that a cash shortage emerged after the APPELLANT left a post office without handing over charge. The APPELLANT argued that dishonest intent and entrustment were unproved, that a substantial cash transfer lacked proper authorization, and that seizure evidence was defective. The RESPONDENT relied on the APPELLANT's responsibility for the office. The case involved section 409 of the Penal Code and section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947.
explanation: The court found that the prosecution established a postal cash shortage but did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the missing money was entrusted to or under the dominion of the APPELLANT and dishonestly appropriated. No witness saw the APPELLANT take or convert the money. Evidence of a large transfer did not establish its delivery to the office, and the depositor's evidence did not show personal receipt by the APPELLANT. Missing records and deficiencies concerning authorization, remittance and custody left an essential evidentiary gap. Absence and failure to hand over charge created suspicion, not proof of criminal breach of trust.

input_summary: The APPELLANT challenged the special judge's judgment dated 8 September 2024 concerning conviction, sentence and confiscation for acquiring assets allegedly disproportionate to known income. The APPELLANT sought relief from the conviction and confiscation against the STATE and a RESPONDENT. The prosecution alleged that assets came from illegal activities of PERSON_1, the APPELLANT's husband. The APPELLANT argued that her assets were declared for tax and came from gifts, family support and savings, including assistance from PERSON_2, her father. The RESPONDENT argued that she failed to establish her father's source of income. The parties referred to the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, including section 27.
explanation: The court found contradictions between the initial complaint and the charge sheet, as well as inconsistencies in the informant and investigating officer's evidence about the APPELLANT's sources of income. It noted that the officer had not examined the father's tax records despite information about gifts appearing in the APPELLANT's tax file. The court considered the prosecution's evidence insufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt and referred to a precedent concerning gifted property. It also treated the earlier discharge of the APPELLANT's husband, a co-accused, as relevant to equal treatment under section 27 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act.

High Court Division 
(Civil Revisional Jurisdiction) 
Present: 
Mr. Justice Md. Riaz Uddin Khan

IN THE MATTER OF :

Md. Riaz Uddin Khan, J: 
 
 
At the instance of the defendant No.1, the 
Bangladesh Railway Rule was issued asking the opposite 
party-plaintiff to show cause as to why the Order No.1 
dated 
01.08.2004 
passed 
by 
the 
District 
Judge, 
Lalmonirhat in Other Appeal No. 28 of 2004 should not 
be set aside and or such other or further order or 
orders should not be passed as to this Court may deem 
fit and proper.  
At the time of issuance of the Rule this court 
was pleased to stay all further proceedings of Other 
Appeal No. 28 of 2004 and the judgment and decree dated 
24.11.2003 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, 
Lalmonirhat in Other Suit No. 68 of 2002 for a period 
of 06(six) months initially which was lastly extended 
on 21.05.2006 for a further period of 6 months.  

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
Facts for disposal of this Rule in brief is 
that the opposite party No.1 filed Other Suit No. 68 of 
2002 against the defendant Bangladesh Railway and 
others for declaration that the judgment and decree 
dated 28.09.1997 (decree signed on 05.10.1997) passed 
in Other Suit No. 117 of 1994 is collusive and not 
binding upon the plaintiff. The suit was contested by 
the defendant Bangladesh Railway and the trial court 
upon hearing both the parties was pleased to decree the 
suit by his judgment and decree dated 24.11.2003 
(decree signed 30.11.2003).  
Against 
that 
judgment 
and 
decree 
dated 
24.11.2003 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, 
Lalmonirhat in Other Suit No. 68 of 2002 the Bangladesh 
Railway filed Other Appeal No. 28 of 2004 before the 
court of District Judge, Lalmonirhat. In filing the 
said Other Appeal there was a delay of 168 days for 
which the appellant Bangladesh Railway filed a separate 
application for condoning the delay under section 5 of 
the Limitation Act. The learned District Judge by his 
impugned 
order 
dated 
01.08.2004 
rejected 
the 
application for condonation of delay of 168 days.  
Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the 
said order dated 01.08.2004 passed by the District 
Judge, Lalmonirhat the defendant Bangladesh Railway 
filed the instant revision and obtained the Rule and 
interim order as stated at the very outset.  
It may be mentioned here that this Court while 
issuing the Rule was pleased to call for the record of 
the lower courts.  
No one appears to support or oppose the rule 
when the matter was taken up for hearing.  

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
I have perused the revisional application. I 
have also examined the lower court records specially 
the application filed under section 5 of the Limitation 
Act for condoning delay of 168 days filed before the 
learned District Judge. I have carefully examined the 
impugned order.  
The learned District Judge by the impugned 
order in a slipshod manner rejected the application for 
condonation of delay on the finding that the defendant-
appellant received certified copy of the judgment and 
decree on 11.02.2004 but filed the appeal in delay of 
168 days which is not properly explained. 
The 
superior 
Courts 
of 
this 
subcontinent 
including ours, in dealing with the application for 
condoning delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 
settled some principles. In the case of Bangladesh Vs 
Jaheruddin [1986 BLD (AD) 180] our Supreme Court, 
Appellate Division observed: “In matter of condonation 
of delay Government does not enjoy any special 
privilege, but the fact remains that due to the 
necessity to obtain opinions of various authorities 
concerned before filing an appeal, some time may 
reasonably be expected to elapse which in the case of 
an individual does not happen. Some consideration in 
appropriate circumstances may, therefore, be extended 
to Government appearing as a litigant. In saying so, no 
rule is being laid down for not observing strictness of 
the proof of substantial and reasonable cause in making 
such delay. Standard of acceptance must, however, 
remain the same in case of both citizens and State.” In 
the case of Government Vs Alauddin being dead his heirs 
[6 BLC (AD) 101] the apex Court observed: “As litigant 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
the government stands on the same footing with ordinary 
litigants, yet, considering the difficulties of the 
Government at various stages, we take sympathetic and 
lenient view and allow consideration of delay of 
Government cases in many cases.” In the case of 
Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag and others Vs Mst 
Katiji and others [AIR 1987 SC 1353] the Indian Supreme 
Court, adopted a liberal approach condoning the delay 
which was referred in approving note by our Supreme 
Court in 59 DLR (AD) 1 wherein it has been stated that- 
1. Ordinarily a litigant does not stand to benefit by 
lodging an appeal late, 2. Refusing to condone delay 
can result in a meritorious matter being thrown out at 
the very threshold and cause of justice being defeated. 
As against this when delay is condoned the highest that 
can happen is that a cause would be decided on merits 
after hearing the parties, 3. “Every day’s delay must 
be explained” does not mean that a pedantic approach 
should be made. Why not every hour’s delay, every 
second’s delay? The doctrine must be applied in a 
rational common sense pragmatic manner, 4. When 
substantial justice and technical considerations are 
pitted against each other, cause of substantial justice 
deserves to be preferred for the other side cannot 
claim to have vested right in injustice being done 
because of a non-deliberate delay, 5. There is no 
presumption that delay is occasioned deliberately, or 
on account of mala-fides. A litigant does not stand to 
benefit by recording delay. In fact, he runs a serious 
risk, 6. It must be grasped that judiciary is respected 
not on account of its power to legalise injustice on 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
technical grounds but because it is capable of removing 
injustice and is expected to do so. 
I respectfully agree with the above principles 
in dealing with condoning delay and fully endorse it.  
In the light of above principles should the Court 
condone the delay occurred in the instant case in 
filing appeal? In the present case on perusal of the 
application filed under section 5 of the Limitation Act 
for condonation of delay of 168 days the petitioner 
Bangladesh Railway, a Government body, clearly stated 
the reasons for delay. The petitioner explained that 
being a statuary body there is a process in filing 
appeal i.e after obtaining certified copy of the 
judgment and decree the petitioner sought advice from 
their legal adviser, after obtaining the advice there 
was process for arranging necessary expenses and after 
approval of such expenses the learned advocate for the 
appellant-petitioner after taking instruction drafted 
the memorandum of appeal along with the application for 
condonation of delay and by that way 168 days delay was 
occurred. 
Such 
explanation, 
in 
my 
view, 
was 
satisfactory as it explained ‘sufficient cause’ and as 
such the learned District Judge should have allowed the 
application condoning the delay. The learned District 
Judge failed to consider that on account of an 
impersonal machinery, i.e Bangladesh Railway, no one in 
charge of the matter is directly hit or hurt by the 
judgment sought to be subjected to appeal, and the 
inherited bureaucratic methodology imbued with note-
making, file pushing, and passing-on-the-buck ethos, 
delay on its part is not difficult to understand. The 
petitioner (appellant) being a statuary body challenged 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
a substantive judgment and decree of the trial court 
and the appellate court should have condoned the delay 
with the end in view to do evenhanded justice on 
merits.  
In such view of the matter as discussed above, 
the impugned order being passed not in correct 
appreciation of law in given facts, I find merits in 
this Rule to interfere with the impugned order passed 
by the learned District Judge.  
In the result the Rule is made absolute. There 
will be no order as to cost.  
The impugned order dated 01.08.2004 passed by 
the District Judge, Lalmonirhat in Other Appeal No.28 
of 2004 is hereby set aside and the delay of 168 days 
in filing Other Appeal No.28 of 2004 is condoned.  
The interim order passed earlier by this Court 
stands vacated.  
The court of appeal below is directed to 
proceed with the appeal in accordance with law 
expeditiously after notifying all the parties keeping 
in mind that the appeal was filed in the year 2004.  
Send down the lower court records along with a 
copy of this judgment at once.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Ziaul Karim 
Bench Officer

petitioner before the learned District Judge was a

Appeal was dismissed by the court of appeal below on 
different ground. Against that dismissal order this Rule

However, the petitioner obtained a interim order by a 
Single Bench of this Court to deposit 10% decretal amount 
which was also in violation of the Supreme Court of 
Bangladesh (High Court Division) Rules, 1973.

provides specific provision for setting aside the ex parte 
decree being a special law there is no scope to direct the 
defendant to deposit 10% of the decretal amount beyond the 
prescribed time as per section 19(2) and 19(3) of the Ain, 
2003. In the case of Pubali Bank Ltd Vs Bangladesh and 
others reported in 66 DLR 317 it is observed: “Therefore,

complementary to each other and has to be read together. As

such, to file an application for setting aside ex parte

provisions i.e section 19(2) and 19(3) of the Ain, must be 
complied with. In other words, to file such application the 
defendant has to satisfy the Adalat about limitation period 
as per requirement of section 19(2) of the Ain and he is 
also required to comply the provision of section 19(3) of 
the Ain i.e deposit of 10% of the decretal dues and that 
the Adalat has no scope to consider such application if any 
of the aforesaid conditions is left in filing the 
application.”  In the case of Osman Gazi Chowdhury Vs Artha 
Rin Adalat reported in 21 BLC 322 it has been observed: 
“Because of the percentage of deposit being only 10% of the 
decretal 
amount, 
the 
time-limitation 
of 
filing 
the 
application being sufficient (30 days from the date of 
knowledge of passing the ex parte decree plus further 15 
days for deposit) and the mode of payment being flexible, 
for, it is permissible to pay in cash or submit bank draft, 
pay order, cheque and any other negotiable instrument, it 
would not be irrational to view these conditions as 
affordable for an aggrieved party.” In an unreported case 
of Prime Global Limited and others Vs. Sonali Bank Limited 
and others in Civil Appeal No. 86 of 2015 the Supreme 
Court, Appellate Division held that- “Thus, it is apparent

<<PAGE 11>>

11
that 
the 
Adalat

decretal amount is to be deposited within 15 days of filing 
thereof.” In those decisions it has been clearly spelt out 
that the Artha Rin Adalat had no jurisdiction to allow such 
application filed by the defendant-petitioner (judgment 
debtor) for setting aside an ex parte decree without 
following the provisions under section 19(2) and 19(3) of 
the Ain. 
The decisions cited by the learned advocate for the 
petitioner, i.e [10 MLR (AD) 186], [1992 BLD (AD) 156] and 
[47 DLR 326], all of which have been passed not in any 
special law rather under Code of Civil Procedure and as 
such those are distinguishable from the present case.  
In such view of the matter we have no option but to 
discharge the Rule.  
Resultantly, the Rule is discharged. However, there 
will be no order as to cost.  
The order of stay earlier granted by this Court 
stands vacated.

<<PAGE 12>>

12
The trial court is at liberty to proceed with the 
execution case without any further delay keeping in mind 
that it was filed in the year 2016.

input_summary: The REVISIONIST, a borrower and original defendant, challenged the district judge's order dated 21 August 2016 concerning an application to reopen an ex parte loan recovery decree in favor of the OPPOSITE PARTY. The REVISIONIST sought restoration of the suit for a contested hearing, asserting that only part of the loan was received and some repayment had been made. The REVISIONIST argued that the statutory time limits were directory and pointed to a subsequent deposit of ten percent of the decretal amount. The OPPOSITE PARTY argued that the application and deposit were late. Both sides relied on section 19 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.
explanation: The court held that sections 19(2) and 19(3) of the special statute must be read together: an application concerning an ex parte decree must satisfy the prescribed time limit and the ten percent deposit must be made within fifteen days of the application. The REVISIONIST did not deposit the amount within that period, and a later deposit could not cure the failure. The court also held that section 20 did not permit an appeal against the relevant interlocutory order and distinguished decisions concerning ordinary civil procedure from this special statutory scheme.

input_summary: The REVISIONIST, an original plaintiff, challenged the revisional court's order dated 30 October 2019 concerning a stay of execution of an earlier land decree against the OPPOSITE PARTIES. The REVISIONIST sought to maintain the stay while a suit seeking a declaration that the earlier decree was not binding proceeded. The REVISIONIST argued that the suit and execution involved the same land and that completing execution would prejudice the pending suit. The OPPOSITE PARTY contended that the REVISIONIST claimed through an earlier judgment debtor and sought neither a declaration of title nor an injunction. The revision was brought under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure.
explanation: The court explained that section 115(4) permits intervention for an error on an important question of law causing an ultimate failure of justice. It found that the REVISIONIST claimed the land through a judgment debtor in the earlier proceedings and sought only a declaration that the earlier decree was not binding, rather than a declaration of title. On that basis it considered the lower revisional court's treatment of the requested execution stay correct. The REVISIONIST had identified no legal error meeting the statutory threshold.

not

the instant Rule which is destined to fail.

input_summary: The REVISIONIST, a defendant in a partition suit, challenged the revisional court's order dated 24 February 2022 concerning restoration of proceedings following an ex parte decree against the OPPOSITE PARTIES. The REVISIONIST sought restoration of the suit, arguing that exceptional circumstances justified use of the court's inherent powers and that a cost had been paid. The OPPOSITE PARTIES argued that the REVISIONIST had an appeal remedy, did not diligently pursue the case and that the trial court acted without hearing them. The parties relied on section 151, Order IX rule 13 and Order XLIII rule 1(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure.
explanation: The court held that dismissal for default of an application to challenge an ex parte decree is appealable under Order XLIII rule 1(d). Although section 151 may exceptionally be invoked, the REVISIONIST showed no special circumstances warranting its use. The court found a lack of diligence, including failure to appear when the matter was heard and failure to pay costs in time. It also applied the section 115(4) threshold for interfering with a lower revisional decision and found no qualifying error on an important question of law.

by his order dated 10.02.2008 was pleased to reject the 
application filed under Order-VII, Rule-11 read with 
Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Against the 
said order dated 10.02.2008 passed by the Assistant 
Judge the defendant-petitioner field Civil Revision No. 
68 of 2008 before the District Judge, Dhaka which was 
ultimately heard by the Additional District Judge, 8th 
Court, Dhaka who after hearing was pleased to reject 
the Revision by his impugned judgment and order dated 
13.07.2009. 
Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the 
said judgment and order dated 13.07.2009 the defendant 
field the instant Civil Revision under section 115(4) 
of the Code of Civil Procedure before this Court and 
obtained the leave and order of stay as stated at the 
very outset. 
No one appears to press or oppose this leave 
granting order when this matter was taken up for 
hearing. 
I have gone through the revision application 
along with the documents annexed therewith. I have also 
carefully examined the order passed by the trial court 
as well as the impugned judgment and order passed by 
the Additional District Judge. 
The defendant-petitioner took as many as seven 
grounds to assail the judgment and order passed by the 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
courts below. The main contention of the defendant-
petitioner is that the present suit is barred by 
Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure as res 
judicata since the matter was earlier substantially 
adjudicated between the parties. The further contention 
of the petitioner is that the matter in dispute was 
finally dissolved in Title Suit No. 82 of 1995 earlier 
hence the suit is barred by the principle of res 
judicata. The further contention of the petitioner is 
that since two execution cases are pending being 
Execution Case No. 02 of 2002 and Execution Case No. 03 
of 2003, those two execution cases should be first 
disposed of before this suit. The last contention of 
the petitioner is that from the averments of the plaint 
it is clear that the present suit is barred by 
principle of res judicata. 
At this stage it would be profitable if we see 
Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure which deals 
with the principle of res judicata reads as under:  
Section-11. Res Judicata. “No Court shall 
try any suit or issue in which the matter 
directly and substantially in issue has been 
directly and substantially in issue in a 
former suit between the same parties, or 
between parties under whom they or any of 
them claim, litigating under the same title, 
in a court competent to try such subsequent 
suit or the suit in which such issue has 
been subsequently raised, and has been heard 
and finally decided by such Court.”  
From plain reading of the above provision of law 
it is clear that this section prohibits adjudication of 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
the same issue between the same parties more than once. 
This is intended to save litigants from being vexed 
twice and is based on the public policy that there 
should be a finality in litigation. The maxim that no 
one shall be vexed twice presupposes that the issue has 
been fairly and finally decided in a former suit. Once 
an issue has been finally decided, it cannot be re-
agitated between the same parties. 
In the present case the petitioner neither 
annexed the plaint of the Title Suit No. 82 of 1995 nor 
any copy of the decree of that suit. However, it 
appears from the record that the present plaintiff 
along with the present defendant-petitioner Joydhar Ali 
and 07 others filed Title Suit No. 82 of 1995 and got 
decree of 5.39 acres of land and there was no partition 
between the present plaintiff and present defendant of 
that suit regarding their ejmali property. Moreover, 
the plaintiff in her plaint further claimed that she 
did not execute any heba (gift) deed and did not made 
any affidavit before any notary public and the 
defendant Joydhar Ali created those documents which are 
forged. The trial court observed that the issue in 
Title Suit (partition suit) No. 82 of 1995 and the 
issue of the present suit No. 81 of 2003 are completely 
different 
hence 
the 
trial 
court 
rejected 
the 
application under Order-VII, Rule-11 of the Code of 
Civil Procedure. It further appears from the judgment 
of the lower revisional court that it observed that the 
prayer/issue of the Title Suit (Partition Suit) No. 82 
of 1995 and the issue of the present suit are 
different. 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
On careful examination of the materials on 
record available before this Court I find that the 
earlier suit was for partition wherein the present 
plaintiff Karamjan Bibi and the present defendant 
Joydhar Ali both were plaintiffs hence it is absurd to 
say that in the earlier suit the dispute between the 
present plaintiff Karamjan Bibi and the present 
defendant Joydhar Ali was in any way dissolved. 
Furthermore, the present plaintiff raised a question of 
forgery against the defendant Joydhar Ali hence the 
defendant’s contention that the present suit is barred 
by the principle of res judicata has no substance at 
all as the issues are different.  
In the facts and circumstances and the position 
of law as discussed above I find no substance in the 
present civil revision which is liable to be discharged 
for devoid of merit which is destined to fail.  
Resultantly, the Leave/Rule is discharged with 
cost.  
The order of stay earlier granted by this Court 
stands vacated.  
The trial court is directed to dispose of the 
present Title Suit No. 81 of 2003 expeditiously as 
early as practicable keeping in mind that the present 
suit is of in the year of 2003. The Execution Case No. 
02 of 2002 and the Execution Case No. 03 of 2003 shall 
remain stayed till disposal of Title Suit No. 81 of 
2003. 
Communicate the judgment and order at once.  
 
 
 
Ziaul Karim 
Bench Officer
input_summary: The REVISIONIST, a defendant, challenged the revisional court's order dated 13 July 2009 concerning a request to terminate a land suit brought by the OPPOSITE PARTY. The suit concerns a disputed gift deed, an earlier decree and partition. The REVISIONIST sought rejection of the plaint, arguing that the dispute had already been finally decided between the parties and that pending execution cases should be resolved first. The OPPOSITE PARTY alleged that the REVISIONIST created a forged gift deed and affidavit. The application relied on section 11 and Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure; neither side appeared at the revision hearing.
explanation: The court applied section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and found that the matters in the earlier partition suit and the present suit were different. Both current adversaries had been plaintiffs together in the earlier suit, so that suit had not resolved the present dispute between them. The present suit also raised an allegation that the REVISIONIST forged a gift deed and affidavit. The earlier plaint and decree were not annexed to the revision. The court therefore found no basis for the asserted bar of res judicata.

The OPPOSITE PARTY contested the injunction application and appealed the trial court's order. explanation: UNCERTAIN: The final order disposed of the Rule without expressly addressing the challenged appellate order, but directed that the status quo be maintained if the suit remained pending. The court noted that the trial court had found no convincing preliminary evidence of an earlier partition and that construction was taking place on the jointly held land. The district judge had given no reason for suspending the protective order. The court also considered the lengthy passage of time and the absence of information about whether the suit or appeal had concluded.

between the same parties, which was tried simultaneously 
with the instant case, the accused as DW1 admitted in cross-
examination that out of five cheques, two were honored and 
three (including the cheque in the instant case) were 
dishonoured, the law of evidence provides that the admitted 
facts need not be proved, therefore, the learned Joint Session 
Judge ought to have found that the dishonor of the cheque 
proved based on the accused’s admission. 
Section 58 of the Evidence Act, 1872 provides as 
follows: 
“Facts admitted need not be proved- No fact need be 
proved in any proceeding which the parties thereto or their 
agents agree to admit at the hearing, or which, before the 
hearing, they agree to admit by any writing under their hands, 
or which by any rule or pleading in force at the time they are 
deemed to have admitted by their pleadings.

20
Provided that the Court may, in its discretion, require 
the facts admitted to be proved otherwise than by such 
admissions.” 
The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the 
respondent No. 1 argued that when additional evidence was 
recorded on 19.07.2026, although the accused appeared 
before the trial Court, she was not afforded an effective 
opportunity to cross-examine PW1. However, I find no 
substance in his argument. 
It appears from the record that the accused submitted 3 
applications on 15.07.2026 and 19.07.2026. One application 
was under Section 205 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to 
dispense with personal attendance, which was allowed. 
Another one is for adjournment. The accused submitted an 
application under Section 548 of the Code of Criminal 
Procedure to have the certified copy of the order of High 
Court Division and sought adjournment to prefer appeal 
before the Honourable Appellate Division. The accused did 
not cross-examine PW1 and did not seek time for cross-
examination. Even when the attested copy of dishonour slips

and bank statement were produced, no objection was raised 
by the accused. 
It appears from the record that the accused-respondent 
never raised any objection regarding non-submission of the 
‘dishonour slip’ at the time of filing of the complaint petition 
and nothing was found in the order sheets of the learned 
Metropolitan Magistrate and the trial Court, namely 
Metropolitan Joint Sessions Judge, First Court, Dhaka in that 
regard. However, the respondent submits this argument at 
very belated stage during hearing of the instant appeal. So, the 
plea regarding non-submission of the dishonor slip at the time 
of filing the petition of complaint is not acceptable at all. 
Upon a scrutiny of the evidence and the materials on 
record, we find that the learned Court below committed an 
error of law in acquitting the accused merely on the ground 
that the complainant failed to produce and exhibit the 
‘dishonour slip’ issued by the drawee bank. 
Production of the bank’s ‘dishonour slip’/return memo 
is indeed a cogent mode of establishing the fact that the 
cheque was returned unpaid. However, non-production of the 
‘dishonour slip’, by itself, cannot invariably be construed as 

<<PAGE 22>>
 
22
fatal to the prosecution, particularly when the factum of 
presentation and dishonour of the cheque is otherwise borne 
out by the evidence on record and the surrounding 
circumstances of the case. 
Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 
makes the return of the cheque unpaid by the bank one of the 
foundational facts constituting the offence. It does not 
necessarily make the production of such slip the sole and 
exclusive mode of proving dishonour. The question is 
whether, on an overall assessment of the evidence, the 
complainant has succeeded in establishing the factum of 
dishonour by legally admissible and credible evidence. 
In the case before this Court, the learned Court below 
appears to have proceeded on the erroneous premise that, in 
the absence of the ‘dishonour slip’ as an exhibited document, 
the prosecution case necessarily failed. Such an approach, in 
my considered view, amounts to an unduly technical 
appreciation of evidence and has failed to consider the 
prosecution evidence in its entirety. 
The complainant proved the cheque in question and 
deposed categorically that the same was presented for 

<<PAGE 23>>
 
23
encashment but was returned unpaid. His evidence on the 
material particulars remained substantially consistent and was 
not shaken in cross-examination. The subsequent issuance of 
the statutory notice demanding payment of the cheque 
amount, coupled with the failure of the accused to discharge 
the liability within the statutory period, constitutes a relevant 
circumstance which lends assurance to the prosecution case. 
The learned Court below, instead of considering the 
cumulative effect of such evidence, has attached decisive 
importance to the non-production of the ‘dishonour slip’. 
It is also material to note that the statutory presumptions 
arising under Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments 
Act operate in favour of the holder of the cheque, unless the 
contrary is proved. The burden upon the accused is not 
discharged by a mere denial; rather, the accused is required to 
rebut the statutory presumption by adducing evidence 
sufficient to create a probable defence. The learned Court 
below has failed to examine the evidence from this 
perspective and has thereby misdirected itself in law. 
I am, therefore, unable to sustain the finding of acquittal 
solely on the ground of non-production or non-exhibition of 

<<PAGE 24>>
 
24
the ‘dishonour slip’. The impugned judgment discloses a 
material misappreciation of evidence and an erroneous 
application of the law governing prosecution under Section 
138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 
Accordingly, the finding of acquittal recorded by the 
learned Court below is liable to be interfered with. The 
evidence on record, if otherwise found sufficient to establish 
the issuance of the cheque, its presentation, dishonour, service 
of statutory notice and failure of the accused to make payment 
within the statutory period, would warrant reversal of the 
impugned judgment and a finding of guilt against the accused 
under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 
Once the execution of the cheque and signature are 
admitted or proved (as established by Exhibit 1), the burden 
shifts to the accused to rebut this presumption by cogent 
evidence. The mere oral assertion that the cheque was issued 
as ‘security’ or that there was no debt is insufficient in the 
absence of documentary proof or convincing evidence. 
The record reveals that the statutory legal notice 
(Exhibit 3) was duly served and the cheque was dishonored 

<<PAGE 25>>
 
25
due to insufficient funds within the valid period. The learned 
Joint Sessions Judge misdirected himself in placing the initial 
burden on the complainant to independently prove the 
underlying transaction despite the operation of Section 118 of 
the Negotiable Instruments Act.  
The reasoning adopted by the trial Court is legally 
unsustainable and has failed justice. Consequently, I find that 
the complainant-appellant has successfully proved the charge 
under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act against 
accused-respondent No. 1 beyond reasonable doubt. 
In the result, the Criminal Appeal is allowed. 
The judgment and order of acquittal dated 14.03.2018 
passed by the learned Metropolitan Joint Sessions Judge, First 
Court, Dhaka in Metropolitan Sessions Case No. 4394 of 
2013, arising out of C.R. Case No. 2554 of 2012 is hereby set 
aside. 
The accused-respondent No. 1, Nogina Hasin, is found 
guilty of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable 

<<PAGE 26>>
 
26
Instruments Act, 1881. She is hereby convicted and sentenced 
to suffer simple imprisonment for a period of  06(six) months 
and to pay a fine of Taka 25,00,000/-(Twenty-Five Lac), 
equivalent to the cheque amount, which shall be realized from 
her and paid  to the complainant-appellant in accordance with 
law. 
The accused-respondent No. 1 is directed to surrender 
before the trial Court within 30 (thirty) days from the date of 
receipt of a copy of this judgment to serve out the sentence, 
failing which the trial Court shall take necessary steps in 
accordance with law for securing her arrest and execution of 
the sentence. 
Let a copy of the judgment along with the Lower Court 
Record (LCR) be communicated to the Court concerned 
forthwith for information and necessary action.  
 
         
              (Md. Bashir Ullah, J) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Md. Ariful Islam Khan 
Bench Officer
input_summary: The APPELLANT, a complainant, challenged the trial court's judgment dated 14 March 2018 concerning a cheque dishonour charge against the RESPONDENT, seeking a conviction. The APPELLANT alleged that a cheque issued after settlement of stock transactions was returned for insufficient funds and remained unpaid after notice. The RESPONDENT argued that the cheque was security, payment had been made, notice was not properly served and the evidence of dishonour was inadequate. The APPELLANT relied on the cheque, postal records and additional financial records; the RESPONDENT disputed their sufficiency and the opportunity for cross-examination. The parties referred to the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and the General Clauses Act, 1897.
explanation: The court found that the cheque, its dishonour, statutory notice and nonpayment were established. It considered the original financial statement and other evidence sufficient to establish dishonour, noting that the return slip had previously been exhibited. Notice sent to the RESPONDENT's admitted address attracted a presumption of service that was not rebutted. Under section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the presumption of consideration operated in the APPELLANT's favor; the RESPONDENT's unsupported security-cheque explanation did not establish a probable defence. The court also found no substantiated denial of an opportunity to cross-examine on the additional evidence.
