wrongly arrived at a finding that the defendants are possessing the suit 
land and thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the 
decision occasioning failure of justice. He prayed for setting aside the 
impugned judgment and decree passed by the appellate court below.  
The learned Advocate Mr. Feroz Alam, appearing on behalf of 
the defendant opposite parties, submits that the defendants proved 
their possession in the suit land based on the gift by CS recorded 
tenant Kasim Uddin Mollah to Abdul Gani Mridha and from the CS 
record to till today, the defendants are possessing the suit land and the 
Appellate Court below legally held that without praying for recovery 
of possession a suit for declaration of title is not maintainable in law. 
He prayed for discharging the Rule. 
I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate Mr. 
Muhammad Musa, who appeared on behalf of the petitioners, and the 
learned Advocate Mr. Feroj Alam, who appeared on behalf of the 
opposite parties, the evidence adduced by both the parties, the 
impugned judgments and orders passed by the courts below, and the 
records.  
On perusal of the evidence reveals that Kasim Uddin Mollah 
was the CS recorded tenant of 77 decimals of land appertaining to CS 
Khatian No. 74, Dag No. 1226 and 24 decimals of land, CS Khatian 
No. 1307, Dag No. 1035. It is an admitted fact that Abdul Jalil Mulla 
is the only son of Kasim Uddin Mollah. The plaintiffs denied that Peta 
and Pachi are not the daughters of Kasim Uddin Mollah. D.W. 1 
stated that Kasim Uddin Mollah died intestate, leaving behind his son 
Abdul Jalil Mollah and two daughters, Peta and Pachi, and Abdul 
Gani Mridha is the husband of Peta.  

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
It is a settled proposition that both the plaintiffs and defendants 
shall prove their respective cases. The defendants admitted that Abdul 
Jalil Mollah is the only son of Kasim Uddin Mollah. The plaintiffs 
denied that Peta and Pachi are daughters of Kasim Uddin Mollah. 
Therefore, the defendants shall prove that Peta and Pachi are the 
daughters of Kasim Uddin Mollah.  
Both the Courts below, on considering the evidence of both the 
parties, arrived at a concurrent finding of facts that the defendants 
failed to prove that Peta and Pachi are the daughters of Kasim Uddin 
Mollah. In the plaint, it has been asserted that Peta, wife of Abdul 
Gani Mridha, is the mother of the defendants. In reply to a question, 
D.W.1 admitted that Turas Ullah Sheikh is his maternal grandfather, 
but in reply to a question by the trial court, he affirmed that his 
mother’s name is Peta. D.W. 1 admitted that Turas Ullah Sheikh is his 
maternal grandfather. Therefore, Peta, daughter of Kasim Uddin 
Mollah, cannot be the mother of D.W.1. I am of the view that the 
statement made by D.W.1 that he is the son of Peta is a lie.  
In reply to a question, D.W. 1 affirmed that the house of his 
grandfather is situated at Faridpur, but from the address of P.W.1 and 
D.W.1, it appears that they are residents of Mohadevpur, Magura, 
which proves that Kasim Uddin Mollah is a resident of 
Mohammadpur Thana who is not the maternal grandfather of 
defendant No.1. D.W. 1 stated that Kasim Uddin Mollah gifted the 
suit property in favor of Abdul Gani Mridha and Abdul Jalil Mollah. 
During cross-examination, D.W.1 Mustafa Mridha, son of late Abdul 
Gani Mridha, admitted that he had no personal knowledge of the gift 
of the suit land by Kasim Uddin Mollah to Abdul Gani Mridha and 
that there is no document or evidence regarding the gift. Nothing has 
been stated by D.W.1 that he heard from his father that Kasim Uddin 
Mollah gifted the suit land to Abdul Gani Mridha. I am of the view 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
that the defendants failed to prove that Kasim Uddin Mollah gifted the 
suit land to Abdul Gani Mridha, and both the courts below, 
considering the evidence of both the parties, rightly arrived at a 
finding that the defendants failed to prove that Kasim Uddin Mollah 
gifted the suit land to Abdul Gani Mridha. There is no scope to hold 
the view that the defendants are possessing the suit land on the basis 
of gift by Kasim Uddin Mollah.  
It is the consistent case of the defendants that they are 
possessing the land on the basis of the gift in 1935 by Kasim Uddin 
Mollah to Abdul Gani Mridha. Since the defendants failed to prove 
the gift, it cannot be said that they are possessing the land based on 
the gift. Although in the written statement, the defendants claimed 
adverse possession of the suit land, none of the DWs stated that the 
defendants got title on the basis of adverse possession in the suit land. 
The trial court found that the plaintiffs own the suit land. 
Admittedly, no rent receipt is proved by either party. The trial 
court held that Abdul Jalil Mollah is the only son of Kasim Uddin 
Mollah and there is no basis of the SA record prepared in the name of 
Abdul Gani Mridha. The appellate court affirmed the finding of the 
trial court that the defendants failed to prove the gift in favor of Abdul 
Gani Mridha by Kasim Uddin Mollah, and that Abdul Jalil Mollah is 
the only heir of Kasim Uddin Mollah. I am of the view that Abdul 
Jalil Mollah is the only heir of Kasim Uddin Mollah and he got title to 
the suit land as the only heir of Kasim Uddin Mollah.  
D.W. 1 tells a lie that he is the son of Peta. No rent receipt is 
proved by either party. The possession of the plaintiffs on half of 
50.50 decimals of land is admitted by the defendants, but the plaintiffs 
denied the possession of the defendants in the suit land. In the absence 
of any documentary evidence regarding payment of tax of the suit 
land by the defendants, it cannot be said that the defendants are 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
possessing the suit land. Furthermore, D.W. 1 tells a lie that Peta is his 
mother. The defendants failed to prove their possession on the basis of 
the gift in 1935.  
I am of the view that the SA Khatian Nos. 98/1515 and RS 
Khatian Nos. 1523/1710 were prepared illegally in the name of Abdul 
Gani Mridha without any basis and the appellate court below failed to 
assess the evidence of both the parties in juxtaposing and misread the 
material evidence adduced by both the parties and arrived at a wrong 
decision as to the possession of the defendants in the suit land and 
thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision 
occasioning failure of justice. The plaintiffs proved their title and 
possession of the suit land, and they are entitled to get a decree of 
declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the suit land. 
The finding arrived at by the appellate court that the suit is not 
maintainable in law is hereby set aside.  
The findings arrived at by the trial court that the plaintiffs have 
title and possession in the suit land are hereby affirmed. 
 I find merit in the Rule. 
In the result, the Rule is made absolute. 
The impugned judgment and order passed by the appellate 
Court is hereby set aside.  
However, there will be no order as to costs.  
Send down the LCR at once.
input_summary: The REVISIONISTS, plaintiffs claiming inherited land, challenged the appellate court's judgment dated 27 June 2022 concerning their title and possession suit against the OPPOSITE PARTIES. They sought restoration of the trial court's declaration, arguing that their predecessor was the sole heir of the recorded owner and that the OPPOSITE PARTIES had not proved a gift or the alleged family relationships. The OPPOSITE PARTIES claimed possession through an earlier gift and argued that a declaration suit required a prayer for recovery of possession. The REVISIONISTS invoked section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, with no other statute identified in the reported submissions.
explanation: The court found that both lower courts had concluded that the OPPOSITE PARTIES failed to prove the alleged gift and family relationships supporting their claim. Their witness lacked personal knowledge of the gift and gave inconsistent evidence about ancestry. Neither side proved rent receipts, and the court found the OPPOSITE PARTIES' possession unproved on the evidence. It accepted the REVISIONISTS' predecessor as the recorded owner's sole heir and concluded that the appellate court had misread material evidence concerning possession and maintainability.

input_summary: The REVISIONISTS, plaintiffs in a title suit against the STATE, challenged the appellate court's order dated 11 March 2025 concerning the addition of OPPOSITE PARTIES as co-appellants in the STATE's appeal. They sought relief from that order after objecting to the addition application. The underlying dispute concerns a declaration of title to property. The OPPOSITE PARTIES applied to join the appeal under Order I rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, while the REVISIONISTS filed a written objection. Neither side appeared at the revision hearing, and the judgment does not describe the detailed grounds of their respective positions.
explanation: The court examined the appellate order and found that it gave no reasons for adding the OPPOSITE PARTIES as co-appellants. Because the order was non-speaking, the court considered it necessary for the appellate court to address the addition application again and provide reasons in accordance with law. The court did not itself decide whether the proposed parties should ultimately be added; it directed the appellate court to make a reasoned order within the specified period.

input_summary: The REVISIONIST, a defendant in a partition suit, challenged the revisional court's order dated 30 January 2025 concerning applications to terminate the suit and amend the plaint. The REVISIONIST sought relief from the lower courts' orders, arguing that an earlier decree involving the parties' predecessors barred the suit under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The OPPOSITE PARTIES alleged that the earlier decree and a deed involved fraud and false personation, and sought amendments to contest them. They argued that the termination application raised no proper case and that no written objection to amendment was filed. The parties also referred to section 151 and Order VI rule 17 of the Code.
explanation: The court found that the REVISIONIST's application introduced factual matters requiring evidence at trial. The proposed amendment was needed to adjudicate the dispute and would not change the suit's nature; no written objection to it had been filed. The lower courts had therefore acted lawfully on both applications. The court further held that the revision under section 115(4) was not maintainable because leave had not been sought or obtained before the Rule issued. It nevertheless continued the status quo concerning the land until the suit's disposal.

5
Learned Senior Advocate Mr. Khair Ezaz Maswood, appearing along with 
the learned Advocate Mr. Sk. Sharifuddin on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 
1(Ka) to 1(Ga) submits that Mohor, son of Jamirdi Sheikh, inherited 20 decimals 
of land of C.S. Khatian No. 368, C.S. Dag No. 2736 out of 78 decimals of land 
and by deed No. 315 dated 06.01.1967 (exhibit 4) Alauddin @ Alfaz, son of

Sheikh. In the absence of evidence, this Court is unable to arrive at a finding as to

Jamirdi Sheikh, in Dag No. 2736.  
Although MROR (S.A.) Khatian No. 915, Dag Nos. 2736, 2611 and 2612 
were jointly prepared in the name of Mohor, Bohor and Mokku Sheikh along with 
their three uncles, but on perusal of Deed No. 10891 dated 24.12.1966 (exhibit Ja)

Sheikh, sold 10 decimals of land of Dag No. 2736 and 65 decimals of land of 
other dag to their brother Bohordi Sheikh, son of Jamirdi Sheikh, which is not 
disputed by the plaintiff. The above evidence depicts that the MROR (S.A.) 
Khatian No. 915 was wrongly prepared, excluding three daughters of Jamirdi 
Sheikh, i.e. (1) Surman, (2) Jarimon and (3) Karimon.  
Alal Uddin @ Alfaz, son of Mohor, transferred 20 decimals of land of Dag 
No. 2736 by deed No. 315 dated 06.01.1967 (exhibit 4) without stating any basis 
of inheritance from his father Mohor to Ujir Ali and Nazir Uddin @ Nazir. By 
amending the written statement, the defendant No. 1 asserted that in an amicable 
partition, Jamirdi Sheikh obtained the suit land. It is found that the plaintiff 
prayed for declaration of title on 15 decimals of land of C.S. Khatian No. 368, 
Dag No. 2736. In deed No. 9516 dated 08.10.1996 (exhibit Gha), it has been 
stated that Dulal Miah and Jalal Miah sold 5 decimals of land purchased by their 
father, Bohordi Sheikh, to Harun-Ar-Rashid by deed No. 10891 dated 24.12.1966 
(exhibit Ja). No record was prepared in the name of Dulal Miah and Jalal Miah, 
sons of Bohordi Sheikh, and Alal Uddin @ Alfaz, son of Mohordi Sheikh. No 
evidence is adduced as to the total land inherited by Mohor from Dag No. 2736 
and subsequently by Alal Uddin @ Alfaz, son of Mohor. Similarly, no statement 
is made in the written statement, or by D.Ws, as to the total land inherited by 
Bohordi Sheikh from Dag No. 2736. I am of the view that there is no basis of 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
ownership of 20 decimals of land sold by Alal Uddin @ Alfaz, son of Mohor, to 
Ujir Ali and Nazir Uddin @ Nazir by deed No. 315 dated 06.01.1967 (exhibit 4) 
and sale of 5 decimals of land by Dulal Miah and Jalal Miah, sons of Bohordi 
Sheikh, in favour of Md. Harun Ar Rashid by deed No. 9516 dated 08.10.1996 
(exhibit Gha) and 5 decimals of land by deed No. 1782 dated 18.02.1997 (exhibit 
Uma) to defendant-petitioner Shahanaz Begum.  
It is found that Alal Uddin @ Alfaz subsequently sold 9 decimals of land 
to Kamal Ahmed, husband of the defendant-petitioner Shahanaz Begum, by deed 
No. 7042 dated 29.06.2005 (Exhibit Cha) without any basis of title. It is apparent 
on the face of the records that there is no clear title of Dulal Miah and Jalal Miah, 
sons of Bohordi Sheikh, and Alal Uddin @ Alfaz, son of Mohordi, regarding the 
total land sold by them from C.S. Dag No. 2736. Therefore, the title of the 
plaintiff and the defendant-petitioner Shahanaz Begum could not be ascertained 
by this Court without partition of 78 decimals of land of C.S. Khatian 368, C.S. 
Dag No. 2736 amongst the heirs of C.S. recorded tenant Bajit Sheikh. I am of the 
view that the suit for declaration of title without partition of 78 decimals of land 
of C.S. Khatian No. 368, Dag No. 2736 amongst the heirs of Bajit Sheikh, the 
present suit for declaration of title is not maintainable. 
The above view of this Court is supported by the decision made in the case 
of Enjaheruddin Mia alias Md. Enjaheruddin Mia Vs. Mohammad Hossain and 
others reported in (1998) 18 BLD (AD) 77 = 50 DLR (AD) 84, in which it has 
been held as under: 
“The proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 
(Act 1 of 1877) provides that no court shall make any 
declaration as to the plaintiff's legal character or his right to 
any property where the plaintiff, being able to seek further 
relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so. So far 
as the instant case is concerned, the plaintiffs could have 
asked for either joint possession or partition as a co-sharer 
of the defendants in the disputed land, but they did not take 
any such stand in the lower appellate Court or even before 
the High Court Division. In such view of the matter it will 
not, at all be fair to put blame either upon the lower 
appellate court or the High Court Division that they did not 
declare plaintiffs’ title to the part of the suit land.” 
In this respect, it is relevant here to rely on a decision made in the case of 
Jahangir Alam (MD) and others vs Sabdir Ahmed and others reported in 22 BLC 

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8
(AD) 75, judgment dated 07.12.2016, in which our Apex Court (Syed Mahmud 
Hossain, J), as his Lordship was then, has held that;  
“The principle expounded in the cases is that in the absence 
of partition of the undivided jote, the plaintiff cannot pray 
for simple declaration of title without praying for partition 
by impleading all the co-sharers. The plaintiff-appellants in 
the case in hand could have asked for joint possession in 
the disputed undivided jote left behind by Samadullah but 
they omitted to do so at any stage of the suit. Thus they are 
not entitled to declaration of title within the specific 
boundary in the undivided jote left behind by Samadullah 
in the absence of left out co-sharers”.....“The plaintiffs, 
without impleading all the heirs of Samadullah, prayed for 
declaration of title in the undivided jote left behind by 
Samadullah. The plaintiffs should have prayed for not only 
declaration of title but also for partition, impleading all the 
co-sharers of Samadullah.” 
In the case of Mrs. Sabiha Khanom vs Jaitun Bibi @ Mrs. Syed Moazzem 
Hossain being dead, her heirs: Syed Nurul Hasan, (1998) reported in 3 MLR (AD) 
15 = 3 BLC (AD) 175 in which our Apex Court has held as under; 
“It must, however, be said that in the absence of any 
evidence of partition of CS plot No. 42 the plaintiff-
petitioner is not without right and title to his portion of 
purchased land. Admittedly, his purchase is through a co-
sharer. But he cannot claim declaration of title simpliciter 
unless he claims a partition for determining the respective 
shares of the four brothers in CS plot No. 42 and thereafter 
his own share of 0.13 acres therein. Hence, although the 
suit has ultimately been dismissed, the issue is still open, 
and the plaintiff is free to agitate the question of his title 
and entitlement to the specific portion of 0.13 acres from 
CS plot No.42 in a properly framed partition suit.”  
It is found that Surman, Jarimon and Karimon, daughters of Jamirdi 
Sheikh, transferred 10 decimals of land by deed No. 10891 dated 24.12.1966 
(exhibit Ja) to their brother Bohordi Sheikh and the plaintiff, although denied, did 
not dispute said deed executed by three daughters of Jamirdi Sheikh. I am of the 
view that MROR (S.A.) Khatian No. 915, Dag Nos. 2736, 2611 and 2612 (Exhibit 
1) was wrongly recorded, excluding the daughters of Jamirdi Sheikh. MROR 

<<PAGE 9>>
 
9
(S.A.) record is not the basis of title. Therefore, the title of Surman, Jarimon and 
Karimon is not affected due to the wrong record of MROR (S.A.) Khatian No. 
915 (Exhibit 1) excluding Surman, Jarimon and Karimon.  
It is found that MROR (S.A.) Khatian No. 915, Dag Nos. 2736, 2611 and 
2612 (exhibit 1) was wrongly prepared in the name of Mohor, Bohor and Mokku 
along with their three uncles, excluding Surman, Jarimon and Karimon, daughters 
of Jamirdi Sheikh. No record was prepared in the name of Alal Uddin @ Alfaz, 
son of Mohor, and Dulal Miah and Jalal Miah, sons of Bohordi Sheikh. The 
plaintiff claimed title through purchase from Alal Uddin @ Alfaz, and the 
defendant-petitioner claimed title by purchasing 5 decimals of land from Dulal 
Miah, son of Bohordi Sheikh, and 5 decimals of land from Harun-Ar-Rashid, who 
purchased from Dulal Miah and Jalal Miah, sons of Bohordi Sheikh. After selling 
20 decimals of land by Alal Uddin @ Alfaz to Nazir Uddin @ Nazir and Ujir Ali, 
Alal Uddin @ Alfaz again transferred 9 decimals of land by deed No. 7042 dated 
29.06.2005 (Exhibit Cha) to Kamal Ahmed, husband of the petitioner. B.S. 
Khatian No. 3610 in respect of 25 decimals of land was prepared in the name of 
Abdul Gani (Exhibit 2), and 15 decimals of land were recorded in the name of 
Md. Motiur Rahman in Khatian No. 4180 (Exhibit 6). Khatian No. 3373 (Exhibit 
Zha/3) was prepared in respect of 5 decimals of land in the name of Md. Harun Ar 
Rashid, vendor of the defendant Shahanaz Begum. Therefore, the finding arrived 
at by the trial Court that no khatian was prepared in the name of the vendors of 
the defendant-petitioner is incorrect, since both the plaintiff and the defendant 
purchased the land from the heirs of Mohor and Bohor, who are the MROR (S.A.) 
recorded owners. Only the C.S. record is undisputed, and the C.S. recorded owner 
is not bound to prove the basis of such record. The S.A. and R.S. records do not 
create any title, and such records will not prevail over the right and title of the real 
owner. If the plaintiff claims title based on the S.A. or R.S. record, he shall prove 
the basis of such records.   
The above view of this Court is supported by the decision made in the case 
of Guru Charan Mondal and others vs. Sree Bhaba Sindhu Sarkar, and others 
reported in 13 MLR (AD) 6,  in which it has been held that; 
“In view of the fact that the kabala dated 9.5.1927 in favour 
of Chapala Bala is an admitted kabala and it has not been 
set aside by any competent court and in view of the fact 
that the plaintiffs proved their possession and also in view 
of the fact that the High Court Division after taking into 
consideration that the same land though has been recorded 
in R.S. and S.A. Khatian in favour of the defendants, but 

<<PAGE 10>>
 
10
such record will not prevail over the title of the plaintiffs, 
we do not find any reason to interfere with the judgment of 
the High Court Division.” 
 
In this respect I recall the observation made by our Apex Court in the case 
of the Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the 
Deputy Commissioner, Feni Vs. Har Chandra Nath and others, reported in 10 
MLR (AD) 313, in which the Appellate Division has held that;  
“It may be mentioned, the law is now settled that a real 
owner is not required to file the suit merely because his 
land has been wrongly recorded in the record of rights and 
he can very much wait until the person in whose name the 
record of rights has been wrongly prepared raised claim in 
the land of the rightful owner. In the instant case, the 
plaintiffs felt that their title to the land in suit has been 
clouded on and from April 6, 1989, when the Tahsildar 
refused to accept the rent from them, referring to the 
khatian in which their land was recorded in the name of the 
Government, and thereupon they were constrained to file 
the suit seeking declaration of title in the land in suit.”  
On perusal of the deed No. 315 dated 06.01.1967 (Exhibit 4) sold by 
Alauddin @ Alfaz to Uzir Ali and Nazir Uddin @ Nazir and the deed No. 15748 
dated 30.12.1986 (Exhibit 5) sold by  Nazir Uddin @ Nazir, it appears that there 
is no boundary in those deeds. No evidence is adduced regarding partition of 78 
decimals of land of C.S. Khatian No. 368, Dag No. 2736. Nothing has been stated 
in the plaint and by P W 1 as to how the boundary stated in the plaint attracts 
Exhibits 4 and 5.  
Both the Courts below failed to consider that Surman, Jarimon and 
Karimon, daughters of Jamirdi Sheikh, sold 10 decimals of land of C.S. Khatian 
No. 368, C.S. Dag No. 2736 by deed No. 10891 dated 24..12.1966 (exhibit Ja) to 
Bohordi Sheikh, predecessor of the vendors of defendant-petitioner Shahanaz 
Begum and that Bohordi Sheikh also inherited land of suit dag No. 2736 from his 
father Jamirdi Sheikh. The plaintiff failed to prove the basis of ownership of 20 
decimals of land sold by Alal Uddin @ Alfaz, son of Mohor, by deed No. 315 
dated 06.01.1967 (exhibit 4) to Uhir Ali and Nazir Uddin @ Nazir, who sold suit 
land to Abdul Gani, vendor of the plaintiff. Therefore, I am of the view that the 
appellate Court below arrived at a wrong finding that the plaintiff purchased the 
suit land from the person who had title to the suit land.  

<<PAGE 11>>
 
11
On perusal of the evidence, it transpires that the defendant-petitioner 
Shahanaz Begum purchased 5 decimals of land by deed No. 1782 dated 
18.02.1997 (exhibit Uma) and accordingly Khatian No. 3398, Dag No. 2736 was 
recorded in the name of Shahanaz Begum (exhibit Zha/4). She also purchased 5 
decimals of land by deed No. 9363 dated 29.09.1997 (exhibit Chha), and finally, 
Khatian No. 3517, Dag No. 2736 (exhibit Zha) was recorded on 29.12.1998 in her 
name in respect of  10 decimals of land purchased by her through exhibits Uma 
and Chha, and she paid the rent through DCR (exhibit Zha/1). 
  In the written statement, D.W. 1 specifically stated that after purchasing 
5 decimals of land, she filled up the land and constructed a house, and after 
purchasing another 5 decimals of land, she extended the house and constructed a 
tube-well. It has been specifically asserted by D.W. 1 that she got the electric 
connection in the suit land in 2002 and proved the demand note regarding the 
electric connection as exhibit Kha, security deposit regarding the electric 
connection as exhibit Kha/1, the certificate issued by the PDB regarding payment 
of the electric bills as exhibits Ka and Ka/1, and the electric bills as exhibits Ga to 
Ga/95. It has been asserted in the plaint and by P.W. 1 that after purchase, the 
plaintiff is possessing the land, making a R¡fl¡ Ol through his caretaker. No 
statement is made in the plaint and by P.W. 1 that after purchase, he got the 
electric connection in his R¡fl¡ Ol. The electric connection and the subsequent 
payment of electric bills by the defendant-petitioner Shahanaz Begum are not 
disputed by P.W. 1. I am of the view that after purchase 10 decimals of suit land 
in 1997 by Exhibits Umo and Chha, the defendant-petitioner Shahanaz Begum 
has been possessing 10 decimals of land, constructing a house therein. I do not 
find any evidence of dispossession of the plaintiff on 27.04.2009 by Kamal 
Ahmed, husband of the defendant-petitioner Shahanaz Begum. Therefore, the 
finding of the Courts below that before dispossession on 27.04.2009, the plaintiff 
was in possession of the suit land is hereby set aside.   
 In a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession, the 
plaintiff shall prove his possession in and subsequent dispossession from specific 
boundary of the suit land. D.W. 2 Priyatosh Chandra Pal stated that he set up 14 
RCC pillars in the suit land in favour of the defendant No. 1. D.W. 4 stated that 
after purchase, the defendant filled up the land and constructed a house. Both the 
courts below, without considering the exhibits Ka, Ka/1, Kha, Kha/1, Ga to 
Ga/95, Gha, Umo, Chha, Ja and Zha, arrived at a wrong finding as to the 
possession of the plaintiff before alleged dispossession. I am of the view that after 
purchase in 1997, the defendant-petitioner Shahanaz Begum has been possessing 
the suit land, getting an electric connection in her house constructed on 10 

<<PAGE 12>>
 
12
decimals of land, and the plaintiff failed to prove his possession in and subsequent 
dispossession from the suit land.  
 In view of the above evidence, findings and observations, I hold the view 
that both the Courts below, without considering the exhibits Ka, Ka/1, Kha, 
Kha/1, Ga to Ga/95, Gha, Umo, Chha, Ja and Zha, arrived at a wrong decision as 
to the title and possession of the plaintiff before alleged dispossession. The 
impugned judgments and decrees of both the Courts below suffer from 
misreading and non-reading of material evidence and thereby both the Courts 
below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision in decreeing 
the suit, occasioning failure of justice. The title of the parties can only be decided 
after partition of 78 decimals of land of C.S. Khatian No. 368, C.S. Dag No. 2736 
amongst the heirs of Bajit Sheikh. However, purchasers of the suit land or the 
heirs of C.S. recorded tenant Bajit Sheikh are at liberty to file a suit for partition 
regarding 78 decimals of land of C.S. Khatian No. 368, Dag No. 2736. 
With the above findings and observations, the Rule is made absolute. 
The impugned judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below are 
hereby set aside.  
The order of stay granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of 
the Rule on 26.11.2024 is hereby vacated.  
Send down the lower Court’s records at once.
input_summary: The REVISIONIST, a defendant in a land title suit, challenged the appellate court's judgment dated 29 October 2024 concerning title and recovery of possession in favor of the OPPOSITE PARTIES. The REVISIONIST sought relief from both lower court decrees, arguing that her purchases, land records and electricity documents established her possession and that the joint property required partition. The OPPOSITE PARTIES relied on a chain of purchases and alleged dispossession in 2009, arguing that their predecessor's possession made a partition suit unnecessary. The REVISIONIST disputed the boundaries and the opposing predecessor's title. The procedural basis for the REVISIONIST's application was section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.
explanation: The court found that neither side's vendor had established a clear entitlement to the particular portions of the undivided land and that title could not be determined without partition among the relevant heirs. It relied on authorities concerning section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and claims to specific portions of undivided property. The lower courts had overlooked a relevant deed and the REVISIONIST's records, electricity connection and bills. The court found the REVISIONIST had possessed the land after purchase and that the OPPOSITE PARTIES had not proved their predecessor's possession and subsequent dispossession.

passed by the trial court, against which the substituted 
plaintiffs/petitioners obtained the Rule. 
No one appears on behalf of the petitioners. 
The learned Advocate Mr. Quazi Fedous Hasan appearing 
on behalf of the defendant opposite party No.1 submits that at the 
time of execution and registration of the deed No. 6896 dated 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
25.7.2010(exhibit-Kha) the plaintiff Ayzen Bewa was a sound 
lady and before execution and registration of the said deed, the 
plaintiff gifted 33 decimals of land by deed No. 6731 of 2010 in 
favor of his daughter Sofia Begum and she also sold 16.5 
decimals of land by deed No. 6816 of 2010 to Abu Bakkar 
Siddique and after registration of the disputed deed (exhibit-
Kha), the plaintiff sold 33 decimals of land by deed No. 8033 
dated 11.12.2011 to A. Karim and others and also sold 18.5 
decimals of land by deed No. 8032 dated 11.12.2011 in favor of 
her daughter Sofia Begum and the plaintiff voluntarily executed 
and registered the disputed deed and on the influence and 
coercion of the petitioners, the plaintiff filed the suit for 
cancelation of the deed duly executed by the plaintiff and both 
the courts below arrived at a concurrent finding of fact that the 
plaintiff Ayzen Bewa executed and registered deed No. 6896 
dated 25.7.2010(exhibit-Kha) and on correct assessment and 
evaluation of the evidence adduced by both the parties, legally 
passed the impugned judgments and degrees. He prayed for 
discharging the Rule. 
 I have considered the submission of the learned Advocate 
Mr. Quazi Ferdous Hasan, who appeared on behalf of the 
defendant opposite party No. 1, perused the evidence adduced by 
both the parties, the impugned judgments and decrees passed by 
the courts below, and the records.  
On perusal of the evidence, it reveals that the plaintiff, 
Ayzen Bewa, is the mother of defendant Md. Fazlur Rahman. 
P.W. 1 Ayzen Bewa admitted that she transferred 1 bigha of land 
to her elder daughter Sufia, by registered deed, and transferred 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
10 kathas of land to her younger daughter by registered deed. 
She also transferred 10 kathas of land to her son Ibrahim. Fazlu 
took her to the deed writer, and she put her LTI, but the deed was 
not read over to her. She admitted that the plaint was not read 
over to her, but he put her LTI.  
It appears that after execution of the disputed deed, P.W. 1 
Ayzen Bewa also sold 33 decimals of land to A. Karim and 
others by deed No. 8033 dated 11.12.2011 (exhibit-gha) and also 
sold 18.5 decimals of land by deed No. 8032 dated 11.12.2011 
(exhibit-ga) to her daughter Sofia Begum. The said A. Karim is 
the husband of Sofia Begum. At the relevant time,  P.W. 1 Ayzen 
Bewa transferred her property by four deeds, which were not 
disputed by the plaintiff. The above evidence depicts that at the 
time of execution and registration of the deed No. 6896 dated 
25.7.2010 (Exhibit-Kha), Ayzen Bewa was a sound lady of 85 
years, and no question was raised by the petitioners regarding 
other deeds executed and registered by P.W. 1 Ayzen Bewa.  
The Sub-Registrar registers a deed following the 
procedure provided in sections 34, 35, 58 and 59 of the 
Registration Act and, after registration, issues a certificate under 
Section 60 of the said Act as to proper registration of the deed. 
After issuance of a certificate under Section 60 of the 
Registration Act, 1908 regarding the registration of a deed, it is 
to be presumed that the deed has been duly registered in the 
manner provided under the Registration Act and that the facts 
mentioned in the endorsement referred to in Section 59 of the 
Registration Act, 1908 have been complied with. The 
presumption under section 60 of the Registration Act, 1908 is 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
rebuttable. If any person disputes the registration of the deed 
after issuance of the certificate under section 60 of the 
Registration Act, 1908, he may adduce evidence to prove that the 
deed was not executed and registered by the executants of the 
said deed. No evidence is adduced by the plaintiff to prove that 
she did not execute the deed No. 6896 dated 25.07.2010(Exhibit-
Kha). 
P.W. 1 Ayzen Bewa stated that she did not execute and 
register the deed in favour of her son Md. Fazlur Rahman. Mere 
denial of the execution and registration is not sufficient to cancel 
a registered instrument unless the plaintiff proves that she did not 
put her LTI on the deed and in the LTI register of the Office of 
Sub-Registrar. No step has been taken by P.W. 1 to prove that 
she did not put her LTI on the deed and in the register of the 
concerned Office of Sub-Registrar. D.W.3 Md. Azgor Ali 
Mondal stated that he read over the deed to P.W. 1 Ayzan Bewa 
and thereafter she put her LTI on the deed. D.W. 2 stated that he 
identified Ayzan Bewa at the time of registration. D.W.4 Abdus 
Salam is the maternal cousin of D.W. 1 and nephew of P.W.1. 
He stated that P.W. 1 gifted the suit land to his cousin D.W.1. 
The execution and registration of the other deeds by Ayzan Bewa 
were not disputed by either party.  
From the evidence discussed hereinabove, it appears that 
P.W. 1 Ayzen Bewa voluntarily executed and registered the deed 
No. 6896 dated 25.07.2010 (Exhibit-Kha), and both the courts 
below, on correct assessment and evaluation of evidence of both 
parties, arrived at a concurrent finding of facts that the plaintiff 
Ayzen Bewa executed and registered deed No. 6896 dated 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
25.7.2010 (Exhibit-Kha) in favour of her son Md. Fazlur 
Rahman. I do not find any misreading or non-reading of the 
material evidence. 
 I find no merit in the Rule. 
 In the result, the Rule is discharged. 
 However, there will be no order as to costs.

input_summary: The REVISIONISTS, heirs of the original plaintiff, challenged the appellate court's judgment dated 17 October 2023 concerning a disputed gift deed in favor of the OPPOSITE PARTY. They sought cancellation of the deed. PERSON_1, their predecessor and the OPPOSITE PARTY's mother, alleged that while ill she was taken for treatment and her thumb impressions were obtained on papers without a gift being made. The OPPOSITE PARTY argued that PERSON_1 voluntarily executed the registered deed and had made other transfers before and after it. No advocate appeared for the REVISIONISTS at the hearing. Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure provided the basis for this revisional application.
explanation: The court applied the rebuttable presumption arising from the registration certificate under section 60 of the Registration Act. PERSON_1's denial alone did not establish that she had not placed her thumb impression on the deed or the registration record. The deed writer testified that the document was read to her, and an identifying witness supported the registration. The court also considered her undisputed transfers before and after the challenged deed as evidence of her capacity. It found no material misreading in the lower courts' concurrent findings of voluntary execution.

<<PAGE 1>>
Present: 
Mr. Justice Md. Shohrowardi 
Civil Revision Number 1779 of 2001 
Nurul Hoque alias Noor Mohammad Howlader  
The sole petitioner being dead, his heirs are given below: 
1(a) Mrs. Anawara Begum alias Alea (Daughter) and others....Petitioners 
-Versus- 
Munshi Md. Isahak Ali Howlader, opposite party No. 1  
being dead, his heirs are given below:  
1(a) Md. Abul Jafar and others....Opposite parties 
Mr. Anwar Hossain Reza, Advocate with 
Ms. Abeda Gulrukh, Advocate   
....For the petitioners 
Ms. Chowdhury Nasima, Advocate  
 
 
....For the opposite party No. 1  
Heard on 21.06.2026, 22.06.2026 and 23.06.2026  
Judgment delivered on 19.07.2026 
 
On an application filed under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 
1908 Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to 
why the impugned judgment and decree dated 21.10.1999 (decree signed on 
27.10.1999) passed by Subordinate Judge, Court No. 2, Patuakhali in Title Appeal 
No. 7 of 1998 affirming those dated 03.11.1997 passed by Senior Assistant Judge, 
Patuakhali Sadar in Title Suit No. 112 of 1995 dismissing the suit should not be 
set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may 
seem fit and proper. 
The plaint case, in a nutshell, is that Tozambar Ali, Lalsan Bibi alias 
Lalbaru Bibi, Rahimjan alias Kanu Bibi and Sobahan were the S.A. recorded 
tenants of 1.07 acres of land appertaining to S.A. Khatian No. 711 and 1.27 acres 
of land appertaining to S.A. Khatian No. 712 of Mouza Lohalia, Thana-Patuakhali 
Sadar. The plaintiff is the heir of Tozambar Ali. Lalboru died intestate, leaving 
behind her heirs, Isab Hawlader and Sona Ali Hawlader, who inherited the land of 
Lal Baru after her death. After the death of Isaab Hawlader, his sons Halim, 
Harun, daughters Sufia Begum and Firoza inherited the land. After the death of 
the sons and daughters of Lal Baru Bibi, the defendant Nos. 9 to 11 inherited the 
land. The S.A. recorded tenant Sobahan sold 46 decimals of land of Khatian Nos. 
711 and 712 on 13.12.1993, and on 11.06.1975 Lalbaru sold 50 decimals of land 
of said khatians to the plaintiff. Thus, the plaintiff got title and possession of 96 
decimals of land and mutated his name in Mutation Case No. 202/93-94. The 
defendant Nos. 1 and 2 created a false deed on 13.05.1958 in the name of 
Sobahan and Hakim and filed Mutation Case No. 21/93-94 against the record 
prepared in the name of the plaintiff, and by order dated 23.04.1995, the record 
prepared in the name of the plaintiff was cancelled. Consequently, the plaintiff 
filed the suit for declaration that the deed Nos. 4554 and 4555 dated 13.05.1958 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
are illegal, collusive and fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff and also 
prayed for setting aside the khatian prepared in the name of the defendant Nos. 1 
and 2.  
The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying 
the assertion made in the plaint, stating that the plaintiff had no title and 
possession in the suit land and that Katu was the owner of the suit land. After his 
death, his sons Meher Ali, Nazimuddin, Afser, Kani and Saju inherited the land. 
Tozamber, daughters of Lalbaru, Rahimjan and Kanu Bibi, and Maiful Bibi 
inherited the suit land. After the death of Maiful Bibi, her son Sobahan and 
husband Abdul Hakim inherited her share. Sobahan and Abdul Hakim sold 13 
decimals of land by deed No. 4555 dated 13.05.1958 to the defendant Nos. 1 and 
2, and 34 decimals of land by deed No. 4554 dated 13.05.1958 to the defendant 
Nos. 1 and 2, and after purchasing the land, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 took 
possession of the suit land and paid the rent of the suit land. Sobahan did not 
transfer any land to the plaintiff. The suit land was correctly recorded in Review 
Case No. 21PK/93-94, and they are now enjoying the suit land by paying rent.  
During trial, the plaintiff examined 3 P.Ws and the defendants examined 4 
D.Ws. After concluding the trial, the Senior Assistant Judge, Patuakhali Sadar, by 
judgment and decree dated 03.11.1997, dismissed the suit, holding that the 
plaintiff did not pray for a decree of declaration of title and that no decree has 
been prayed for cancellation of the deed Nos. 4554 and 4555 dated 13.05.1958 
(exhibits Kha and Kha/1) and without praying for a decree of declaration of title, 
the suit is not maintainable.  
Against the said judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, the 
plaintiff filed Title Appeal No. 7 of 1998 in the Court of District Judge, 
Patuakhali. The Subordinate Judge, Court No. 2, Patuakhali heard the appeal, and 
by the impugned judgment and decree, affirmed the judgment and decree of the 
trial Court, holding that the S.A. record was not correctly prepared and that the 
plaintiffs failed to prove that deed Nos. 4554 and 4555 dated 13.05.1958 were not 
executed and registered by Sobhan and that after the execution and registration of 
the deed Nos. 4554 and 4555 dated 13.05.1958, Sobhan did not pay the rent and 
that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title and possession and that there was no 
record in the name of Sobhan and no rent has been paid by him and that Sobhan 
did not claim his possession after 1958 against which the plaintiff obtained the 
Rule.  
Learned Advocate Mr. Anwar Hossain Reza, appearing along with the 
learned Advocate Ms. Abeda Gulrukh on behalf of the petitioners, submits that 
after selling the suit land by deed No. 5052 dated 13.12.1993 (exhibit 1) to the 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
plaintiff, the vendor Sobhan handed over possession of the suit land to the 
plaintiff, which is corroborated by P.W. 3 Md. Sobhan Hawlader, and P.W. 3 also 
denied the execution of the deed Nos. 4554 and 4555 dated 13.05.1958, and 
considering the title of the plaintiff, the suit land was correctly recorded in the 
name of the plaintiff by the AC Land, Patuakhali, Sadar. During trial, the plaintiff 
proved their title and possession of the suit land, and the defendant failed to prove 
original deeds purchased by them from P.W. 3 Md. Sobahan Hawlader, and both 
the Courts below, on misreading and non-reading of the material evidence, 
arrived at a concurrent finding of fact that the plaintiff failed to prove title and 
possession of the suit land and thereby the Courts below committed an error of 
law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He prayed 
for making the Rule absolute.  
Learned Advocate Ms. Chowdhury Nasima, appearing on behalf of the 
opposite party No. 1, submits that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 purchased the land 
from Sobahan and Hakim Ali, who are the heirs of Maiful Bibi, C.S. recorded 
tenant of the suit land, by deed Nos. 4554 and 4555 dated 13.05.1958 (exhibits 
Kha and Kha/1), and their names were recorded in khatian, and now possessing 
the suit land, paying rent, and after transfer of the suit land by Sobahan and 
Hakim Ali, there was no title of Sobahan in the suit land to subsequently transfer 
the suit land by deed No. 5052 dated 13.12.1993 (exhibit 1) to the plaintiff. She 
further submits that the plaintiff failed to prove that exhibits Kha and Kha/1 were 
not executed and registered by P.W. 3 Md. Sobahan Hawlader. She also submits 
that the plaintiff did not make any prayer in the plaint for declaration of title and 
cancellation of the deeds (exhibits Kha and Kha/1) and failed to prove their title 
and possession in the suit land, and both the Courts below, on correct assessment 
and evaluation of the evidence, arrived at a concurrent finding of fact that the 
plaintiff had no title and possession on the suit land. She prayed for discharging 
the Rule. 
I have considered the submission of the learned Advocate Mr. Anwar 
Hossain Reza, who appeared along with the learned Advocate Ms. Abeda 
Gulrukh on behalf of the petitioners, and the learned Advocate Ms. Chowdhury 
Nasima, who appeared on behalf of the opposite party No. 1, and have perused 
the evidence adduced by both the parties, the impugned judgments and decrees 
passed by the Courts below, and the records. 
On perusal of the evidence, it reveals that Tozambar Ali, Lalsan Bibi alias 
Lalbaru Bibi, Rahimjan alias Kanu Bibi and Sobhan are the S.A. recorded tenants. 
The case of the plaintiff is that the plaintiff purchased 46 decimals of land of S.A. 
Khatian Nos. 711 and 712 of Mouza Lohalia of Patuakhali Sadar by deed No. 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
5052 dated 13.12.1993 (Exhibit 1) from the S.A. recorded tenant Sobhan. The 
plaintiff also claimed that Nurul Haque purchased 50 decimals of land of S.A. 
Khatian Nos. 711 and 712 from Lalsan Bibi alias Lalbaru Bibi by deed No. 10078 
dated 11.06.1975 (exhibit 1/Ka) and obtained title to 96 decimals of land, which 
was correctly recorded in Mutation Case No. 202/93-94 in the name of the 
plaintiff, but said record was illegally cancelled, recording the name of the 
defendant Nos. 1 and 2 regarding 46 decimals of land. The plaintiff is the son of 
S.A recorded tenant Tozambar. P.W. 1 denied that P.W. 3 Md. Sobahan Hawlader 
did not transfer any land to the plaintiff and that deed Nos. 4554 and 4555 dated 
13.05.1958 (exhibits Kha and Kha/1) were executed and registered by S.A. 
recorded owner Sobahan and Hakim Ali in the name of the defendant Nos. 1 and 
2. The case of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is that they purchased 34 decimals of 
land by deed No. 4554 dated 13.05.1958 (exhibit Kha) of the S.A. Khatian Nos. 
711 and 712 from Sobahan and Hakim Ali Hawlader and 13 decimals of land by 
deed No. 4555 dated 13.05.1958 (exhibit Kha/1) from Sobahan and Hakim Ali, 
who inherited the land from C.S. recorded tenant Maiful Bibi.  
On perusal of the evidence, it further reveals that admittedly Sobahan and 
Hakim Ali are the S.A. recorded tenant of the suit land, and both the plaintiff and 
defendants claimed that they purchased the land from Sobahan and Hakim Ali. 
No statement is made in the plaint that Sobahan and Hakim Ali did not execute 
and register the deed Nos. 4554 and 4555 dated 13.05.1958 (exhibits Kha and 
Kha/1). Since the execution and registration of the said deeds by Sobahan and 
Hakim Ali in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is not denied by the plaintiff 
and no relief is prayed for cancellation of the said deeds, I am of the view that the 
exhibits Kha and Kha/1 were executed and registered by Sobahan and Hakim Ali 
in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2.  
S.A. recorded tenant Md. Sobahan Hawlader is examined as P.W. 3, and 
he denied the execution of the deeds in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, but 
the plaintiff did not take any steps to prove that the exhibits Kha and Kha/1 were 
not executed and registered by P.W. 3 Md. Sobahan Hawlader and Hakim Ali. 
Exhibits Kha and Kha/1 are old registered documents executed and registered in 
1958.  
After issuance of a certificate under section 60 of the Registration Act, 
1908 regarding the registration of a deed, it is to be presumed that the deed has 
been duly registered in the manner provided under the Registration Act and that 
the facts mentioned in the endorsement referred to in section 59 of the 
Registration Act, 1908 have been complied with. The presumption under section 
60 of the Registration Act, 1908 is rebuttable. If any person disputes the 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
registration of the deed after issuance of the certificate under section 60 of the 
Registration Act, 1908, he may adduce evidence to prove that the deed was not 
executed and registered by the executant of the said deed. D.W. 1 produced the 
original deed Nos. 4554 and 4555 dated 13.05.1958, which have been destroyed 
by termites, and proved the certified copy of the said deeds as exhibits Kha and 
Kha/1. Therefore, D.W. 1 legally proved the exhibits Kha and Kha/1 in 
accordance with law. In the instant case, no application has been filed by the 
plaintiff for sending the LTI of P.W. 3 and Hakim Ali on the LTI register kept in 
the office of the concerned Sub-Registrar to the handwriting expert for 
ascertaining that P.W. 3 and Hakim Ali did not execute and register the disputed 
deeds (exhibits Kha and Kha/1).  
As old documents of more than 30(thirty) years, there is a presumption 
under Section 90 of the Evidence Act, 1872 that deed Nos. 4554 and 4555 dated 
13.05.1958 (exhibits Kha and Kha/1) were executed by Sobahan and Hakim Ali 
unless proved by the plaintiff that the said deeds were not executed and registered 
by Sobahan and Hakim Ali. The plaintiff did not take any steps to prove that the 
exhibits Kha and Kha/1 were not executed by Sobahan and his father Hakim Ali 
by sending those exhibits to a handwriting expert. I am of the view that Sobahan 
and Hakim Ali transferred the suit land in 1958 in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 
and 2 by exhibits Kha and Kha/1 and their title passed to the defendant Nos. 1 and 
2, and no title passed by subsequent execution and registration of the deed No. 
5052 dated 13.12.1993 (exhibit 1) in favour of the plaintiff.  
It is a settled proposition that documentary evidence will prevail over oral 
evidence. Oral evidence of P.W. 3 Sobhan Howlader cannot be relied on to hold 
that the registered deed exhibits Kha and Kha/1 were not executed and registered 
by P.W. 3 and his father Hakim Ali without expert opinion. No statement is made 
by P.W. 3 that his father Hakim Ali did not sell the suit land by Exhibits Kha and 
Kha/1.    
Admittedly, the record prepared in the name of the plaintiff was cancelled 
in Review Case No. 21C/93-94. The plaintiff ought to have filed the suit for 
declaration of their title in the suit land and, without praying for declaration of 
title, filed the suit for declaration that the exhibits Kha and Kha/1 are not binding 
on the plaintiff. I am of the view that without declaration of title, the suit in its 
present form is not maintainable in law. The appellate Court found that the 
plaintiff failed to prove his title and possession in the suit land. Since Sobahan 
and his father Hakim Ali transferred the suit land by deed Nos. 4554 and 4555 
dated 13.05.1958 (exhibits Kha and Kha/1) to the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, no title 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
passed to the plaintiff by subsequent deed No. 5052 dated 13.12.1993 (exhibit 1) 
executed by Sobahan.  
P.W. 3 Md. Sobahan Hawlader did not say that he paid the rent after 1958. 
It is found that the defendants paid the rent after purchase and proved the rent 
receipts as Exhibits Cha-Cha14. After transfer of the suit land by Sobahan and 
Hakim Ali in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, they did not pay any rent of 
the suit land, although they are the S.A. recorded tenants, which indicates that 
Sobahan and Hakim Ali transferred the suit land and handed over possession to 
the defendant Nos. 1 and 2.  
In view of the above findings, observations, and the proposition, I am of 
the view that P.W. 3 Md. Sobahan Hawlader and his father Hakim Ali Hawlader 
transferred 34 decimals of land by deed No. 4554 dated 13.05.1958 (exhibit Kha) 
to the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and they also sold 13 decimals of land appertaining 
to S.A. Khatian Nos. 711 and 712 of Mouza Lohalia of Patuakhali Sadar by deed 
No. 4555 dated 13.05.1958 (exhibit Kha/1) to the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and no 
title passed to the plaintiff by subsequent deed No. 5052 dated 13.12.1993 
(exhibit 1), and both the Courts below, on correct assessment and evaluation of 
the evidence, legally passed the impugned judgments and decrees.  
I do not find any misreading or non-reading of material evidence. No 
perverse finding has been arrived at by the Courts below. 
I find no merit in the Rule.   
In the result, the Rule is discharged.  
The ad-interim order of status quo granted earlier is hereby vacated.   
However, there will be no order as to costs. 
Send down the lower Court’s records at once.
input_summary: The REVISIONISTS, heirs of the original plaintiff, challenged the appellate court's judgment dated 21 October 1999 concerning competing land deeds and a mutation record in favor of the OPPOSITE PARTIES. They sought relief from the lower courts' decisions and asserted ownership and possession through purchases, including a 1993 deed. They argued that a vendor denied executing the OPPOSITE PARTIES' earlier deeds and that those parties had not proved the originals. The OPPOSITE PARTY relied on purchases in 1958, possession and rent payments, and argued that the suit lacked necessary prayers for title and cancellation. The revision was brought under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
explanation: UNCERTAIN: The court relied on presumptions under both the Evidence Act and the Registration Act, and no single provision was clearly decisive. It treated the 1958 deeds as proved and invoked the presumption for documents over thirty years old under section 90 of the Evidence Act. The original deeds had been damaged and certified copies were produced; the plaintiff did not obtain expert examination to support the denial of execution. The court found that title had passed to the OPPOSITE PARTIES before the later purchase, noted their rent payments, and considered the suit defective without a prayer for declaration of title.

The prosecution case, in brief, is that on 04.10.2021, one 
Md. Shaim Ahmed, Sub-Inspector (Unarmed), Tejgaon Zonal 
Team, DB, Tejgaon Division, DMP, Dhaka, as informant, lodged 
a First Information Report with Tejgaon Industrial Area Police

in his right hand was conducted, from which 40 bottles of 
Phensedyl, each containing 100 ml and bearing labels and corks, 
were recovered. Thereafter a seizure list was prepared at the 
place of occurrence. Subsequently, the police took the accused

After investigation, the police submitted the charge sheet 
against the accused appellant under Table 14(Kha) appended to

Section 36(1) and 41 of the Madok Drobbo Niyantran Ain, 2018, 
before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. Thereafter, the

As the case was ready for trial, it was transferred to the

Subsequently, 
the 
learned 
Additional 
Metropolitan 
Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, framed the charge against the 
appellant under Tablet 14(Kha) of the Act appended to Section 
36(1) of the Madok Drobbo Niyantran Ain, 2018, which was

pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. 
During the trial, the prosecution examined 11 (eleven)

examined under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 
because he was absent. 
 After the conclusion of the trial, the learned Additional 
Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, by the impugned judgment and

4

Drobbo Niyantran Ain, 2018 and sentenced him to suffer

Mr. Sk. Imran Kabir, the learned Advocate appearing on 
behalf of the convict-appellant, submits that the appellant is 
innocent and has been falsely implicated in the instant case due 
to a conspiracy at the instance of the informant. He further 
submits that no incriminating article was recovered from the 
possession of the appellant and that the alleged recovery of 40 
bottles of Phensedyl has not been proved by reliable and 
independent evidence. Accordingly, he submits that the 
impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence is 
liable to be set aside and the appellant is entitled to be acquitted. 
On the contrary, Mr. Monzurul Alam Sujan, the learned 
Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of the State, 
vehemently opposes the submissions made by the learned 
Advocate for the convict-appellant and submits that the 
prosecution case regarding the recovery of 40 bottles of 
Phensedyl has been duly corroborated by the evidence of the

witnesses. He further submits that the prosecution witnesses

In considering the sentence, however, it noted the APPELLANT's record and treated this as the first criminal case against him, warranting a reduced term and fine.

input_summary: The PETITIONER, a taxpayer, brought a writ against the STATE and RESPONDENTS challenging the tax commissioner's order dated 27 November 2017 concerning correction of an earlier revision order. The PETITIONER sought a declaration that the later order lacked lawful authority. The dispute concerns the classification of investment income and whether tax required before seeking revision had been paid. The PETITIONER argued that tax certificates confirmed payment and that the commissioner lacked authority to review the earlier order. The STATE argued that the income was misclassified and that the correction addressed an unpaid tax liability. The parties relied on the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984, particularly sections 74, 120, 121A and 173.

input_summary: The PETITIONER, an investment recipient, brought a writ against the STATE and tax RESPONDENTS challenging assessment proceedings dated 26 September 2017 and a revision order dated 14 November 2017 for five assessment years. It sought declarations that those actions lacked lawful authority. The PETITIONER maintained that its share of investment proceeds was dividend income, tax had been deducted at source, and reassessment would duplicate taxation; it also questioned the hearing and consideration of its grounds. The STATE argued that the PETITIONER owned no shares, received income from other sources and had not paid the required tax. The parties relied on the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984, including sections 120 and 121A.
explanation: The court read the investment agreement as excluding any ownership of shares by the PETITIONER. Applying the Income Tax Ordinance's definition of dividend, it concluded that the proceeds were income from other sources rather than the PETITIONER's dividend income. It found the section 120 revision of erroneous assessments justified and that notice of the proceedings had been given. It also held that the tax prerequisite for revision under section 121A was unmet. The court considered relevant an unpursued tax reference concerning a later assessment year and found no basis to interfere with the challenged actions.

<<PAGE 1>>
 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BANGLADESH 
HIGH COURT DIVISION 
(CIVIL REVISIONAL JURISDICTION) 
 
Present:     
Mr. Justice Rezaul Karim 
 
Civil Revision No. 633 of 2009 
 
Abdur Rashid Patwri and others 
........ Petitioners 
-Versus- 
 
Mst. Raihana Begum and others 
....... opposite parties 
Mr. Ali Imam Khaled Rahim, Advocate 
…….For the petitioners 
None.  
…….For the opposite parties 
 
 
Heard on: 13.09.2026 
Judgment on: 14.09.2026 
 
On an application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil 
Procedure, 1908 (the Code), this Rule was issued calling upon the 
preemptor opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment 
and order dated 28.1.2009 of the District Judge, Laxmipur passed in 
Civil Revision No. 4 of 2008 reversing the judgment and order dated 
13.2.2008 of the Assistant Judge, Ramganj, Laxmipur passed in 
Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 2007 rejecting the plaint should not be 
set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this 
Court may seem fit and proper. 
 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
 
: 2 : 
At the time of issuance of the Rule, all further proceedings of 
Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 2007, now pending before the Assistant 
Judge, Ramganj, Laxmipur, was stayed for a period of 3 (three) 
months. Subsequently, the order of stay was extended from time to 
time, and it is still in force. 
The Rule was obtained by Abdur Rashid Patwari, the pre-
emptee. He died on 07.11.2012, and his heirs were substituted as 
petitioners Nos. 1(a) to 1(k) by order dated 30.07.2013. Thereafter, 
petitioner No. 1(h), Billal Hossain, died on 01.01.2014, and his heirs 
were substituted as petitioners Nos. 1(h)(I) and 1(h)(II) by order dated 
21.04.2015. 
The facts relevant for disposal of the Rule, in brief, are that on 
17.06.2007 opposite party No. 1, Mst. Raihana Begum, filed 
Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 2007 before the Assistant Judge, 
Ramganj for pre-emption of 24 decimals of land. Her husband, 
opposite party No. 2, had transferred the land to Abdur Rashid 
Patwari by registered deed of exchange No. 2168 dated 18.04.2007. 
The parties and the courts below treated her application as one under 
section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the SAT 
Act). In the application, she stated that she had acquired her share in 
the holding by two registered sale deeds of 1996 and 1998 and by a 
registered deed of exchange of 2002. She described herself as a co-
sharer of the holding by purchase and by exchange, and the pre-

<<PAGE 3>>
 
 
: 3 : 
emptee as a stranger. She alleged that the deed of exchange was in 
truth a sale, made in collusion to defeat her right of pre-emption. 
The pre-emptee contested the case and, on 14.01.2008, filed an 
application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code for rejection of the 
plaint. He stated that the deed was a genuine deed of exchange, that 
under section 96 of the SAT Act as substituted in 2006 only a co-
sharer by inheritance may apply for pre-emption, and only against a 
sale, and that the required deposit had not been made. By order dated 
13.02.2008, the Assistant Judge allowed the application. He held that 
only a co-sharer by inheritance may apply under section 96(1) of the 
SAT Act and only a sale can be pre-empted, whereas the pre-emptor 
had described herself as a co-sharer by purchase and the deed was a 
deed of exchange. He rejected the case and allowed the pre-emptor to 
withdraw her deposit. 
The pre-emptor then filed Civil Revision No. 4 of 2008 before 
the District Judge, Laxmipur under section 115(2) of the Code. By the 
impugned judgment and order dated 28.01.2009, the learned District 
Judge allowed the revision. After recording the submissions of both 
sides, he observed, in two short sentences, that the trial court had 
passed the order without properly understanding the legal question 
and that the order was not correct. He set aside the order and directed 
the trial court to proceed according to law. 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
 
: 4 : 
The learned Advocate for the petitioners made submissions in 
terms of the grounds taken in the revision petition. It was submitted 
that the pre-emptor's own application shows that she is not a co-sharer 
by inheritance, so that her application is barred by the first proviso to 
section 96(1) of the SAT Act, and that the learned District Judge set 
aside a reasoned order without discussing the law. 
No one appeared for the opposite parties when the Rule was 
taken up for hearing, and no counter-affidavit was filed. The Rule has, 
therefore, been heard ex parte. Records were not called for. The 
questions arising in this Rule are questions of law, and they can be 
decided on the certified copies annexed to the revision petition. 
To appreciate the submission of the learned Advocate for the 
petitioners, section 96(1) of the SAT Act, as substituted by section 2 
of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 2006 (Act 
No. XXXIV of 2006), is reproduced below: 
"96. Right of pre-emption.- (1) If a portion or share of a 
holding of a raiyat is sold to a person who is not a co-sharer 
tenant in the holding, one or more co-sharer tenants of the 
holding may, within two months of the service of the notice 
given under section 89, or, if no notice has been served 
under section 89, within two months of the date of the 
knowledge of the sale, apply to the Court for the said 
portion or share to be sold to himself or themselves: 
 
Provided that no application under this section shall 
lie unless the applicant is- 
(a) a co-sharer tenant in the holding by inheritance; and 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
 
: 5 : 
(b) a person to whom sale of the holding or the portion or 
share thereof, as the case may be, can be made under 
section 90: 
 
Provided further that no application under this 
section shall lie after expiry of three years from the date of 
registration of the sale deed." 
 
The deed was registered, and the application was filed, in 2007, 
after the substituted section came into force. Both sides proceeded on 
that footing. The quoted provision shows that, after the amendment, 
the right of pre-emption under section 96(1) of the SAT Act arises 
only where a portion or share of a holding is sold, and that only a co-
sharer tenant in the holding by inheritance may seek it. The words 
"shall lie unless" in the first proviso create a statutory bar. 
Under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code, the court looks only at 
the statements in the plaint and assumes them to be true for the limited 
purpose of that rule. In her own application, the pre-emptor claims to 
be a co-sharer by purchase and by exchange. She nowhere claims to 
be a co-sharer by inheritance. On her own statements, therefore, the 
application is ex facie barred by the first proviso to section 96(1) of 
the SAT Act. 
The main contention of the pre-emptor before the learned 
District Judge was that the deed of exchange was a sale in disguise. 
Whether the deed is a genuine exchange or a sale is a question of fact 
which could not be decided under Order VII, rule 11. But even if her 
allegation is accepted for the limited purpose of the rule, it does not 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
 
: 6 : 
remove the independent bar arising from her own pleaded status. It is, 
therefore, not necessary to decide whether the deed is a sale or an 
exchange. Her reliance on section 96(2) of the SAT Act is also 
misplaced. That sub-section deals with the persons who must be made 
parties to an application. It does not decide who may apply. 
The trial Court, therefore, rightly held that the pre-emption 
application is not maintainable in law, since the pre-emptor is not a 
co-sharer by inheritance. The learned District Judge failed to 
appreciate the law in this regard. He set aside the order of the trial 
Court without dealing with its findings and without assigning any 
cogent reason. The impugned judgment does not disclose any 
consideration of the first proviso to section 96(1) of the SAT Act. 
It should also be mentioned that the revision before the learned 
District Judge was itself incompetent. The petitioners did not raise this 
point. However, it is a question of jurisdiction which appears on the 
face of the record, and a court cannot assume a jurisdiction which the 
law does not give it. Under section 115(2) of the Code, the District 
Judge may revise an order of an Assistant Judge only where it is an 
order from which no appeal lies. The order dated 13.02.2008 was 
appealable on either of two footings. First, the courts below treated 
the pre-emption application as a plaint and the order as one rejecting 
the plaint. Section 2(2) of the Code provides that a "decree" "shall be 
deemed to include the rejection of a plaint", and section 96(1) of the 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
 
: 7 : 
Code provides for an appeal from every decree passed by a court 
exercising original jurisdiction. Secondly, section 96(15) of the SAT 
Act provides: "An Appeal shall lie to the ordinary Civil Appellate 
Court from any order of the Court under this section." The order 
rejecting the pre-emption application was an order of the Court under 
section 96 of the SAT Act. On either view, the remedy of the pre-
emptor was an appeal, not a revision. The learned District Judge ought 
to have found that the revision was incompetent, and it was liable to 
be rejected in limine. Instead, he entertained it without jurisdiction. 
This is an independent ground, and it would by itself be sufficient to 
dispose of the Rule. 
Regard being had to the above, I find that the learned District 
Judge committed an error of an important question of law resulting in 
an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice within the 
meaning of section 115(4) of the Code, on two independent grounds. 
First, he entertained and allowed a revision which did not lie, and 
thereby set aside an appealable order in a proceeding which was not 
maintainable. Secondly, even if the revision had been maintainable, he 
reversed a legally sustainable order without considering the first 
proviso to section 96(1) of the SAT Act, and thereby revived an 
application which, on the pre-emptor's own statements, is barred by 
law. On the other hand, the trial court rightly rejected the pre-emption 
application in so far as it held the application to be barred by the first 

<<PAGE 8>>
 
 
: 8 : 
proviso to section 96(1) of the SAT Act. I have not considered the 
question of deposit under section 96(3) of the SAT Act, which neither 
of the courts below decided. 
In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to 
costs. 
The judgment and order dated 28.01.2009 passed by the learned 
District Judge, Laxmipur in Civil Revision No. 4 of 2008 is hereby set 
aside, and the order dated 13.02.2008 passed by the Assistant Judge, 
Ramganj, Laxmipur in Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 2007 is restored. 
The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule 
stands vacated. 
Communicate the judgment at once. 
 
 
 
 
 
Mazhar, BO

the said credit facilities by execution of a mortgage deed along with an 
irrevocable power of attorney executed by the said defendants, the

application of the defendant No. 2, the said credit facilities were 
subsequently renewed vide sanction advice dated 28.06.2012, allowing

It is not disputed that the impugned judgment and decree dated

the defendant no. 3 in Artha Rin Suit No. 114 of 2017. Section 19 of 

<<PAGE 8>>
 
 
: 8 : 
 
the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 makes specific provision for a 
defendant, against whom an ex parte decree has been passed, requiring 
such defendant to apply, within thirty days of the decree or of acquiring 
knowledge of it, for setting aside such decree upon depositing 10% (ten 
percent) of the decretal amount. It is admitted position based on record 
that the petitioner never used the remedy nor did she prefer an appeal 
under section 41 of the Ain against the judgment and decree. 
Section 20 of the Ain further provides that, save as provided in 
the Ain itself, no court or authority shall entertain any question 
touching any proceeding, order, judgment or decree of an Artha Rin 
Adalat, and that any application for relief made in disregard of the 
provisions of the Ain shall not be entertained by any court or authority. 
The Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is a special law made for the specific 
purpose of speedy realisation of dues owed to banks and financial 
institutions. In the facts of the instant case, where the petitioner has not 
availed of either of the remedy under section 19(2) against the ex parte 
decree or remedy of appeal under section 41, we find that the writ 
petition is not maintainable. 
We are, however, mindful that this bar is not absolute. 
Notwithstanding Section 20 of the Ain, a writ may lie where the 
impugned judgment or decree is shown to be coram non judice, that is, 
passed by a Court having no jurisdiction at all, or passed wholly 
without or in excess of jurisdiction, or is the outcome of fraud practised 
on the court. No such case has been made out in the instant writ 
petition. The grounds urged on behalf of the petitioner, namely, that the 

<<PAGE 9>>
 
 
: 9 : 
 
decree improperly included the mortgaged property in its schedule, and 
that no issue was framed on the point of limitation, are all the issues to 
be adjudicated in the proper forum as discussed above. 
Having availed of neither remedy, the petitioner cannot be 
permitted to invoke the extraordinary writ jurisdiction of this court in 
substitution thereof.  
We are unable to accept the submission that judicial review 
under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution admits of no limitation or 
waiver, and that this alone makes the writ petition maintainable. This 
may be true as a general proposition, but it does not, by itself, answer 
the question before us, namely, whether the petitioner should be 
allowed to invoke the writ jurisdiction of this court without ever having 
taken the specific remedy that the Ain itself gave her for the very 
wrong of which she now complains.  
We are of the view that, if the petitioner has any grievance 
regarding the alleged misapplication of Section 47 of the Ain, the same 
cannot be agitated in the writ jurisdiction. Rather, the petitioner ought 
to have availed the appropriate statutory remedy by way of an appeal in 
the form of a miscellaneous case under section 41 and 19 of the Ain.  
For the reason stated above, we do not find any substance in the 
submission and the same is rejected. 
Regard being had to the above facts and circumstances, we do 
not find any merit in the instant writ petition which is also not 
maintainable. 

<<PAGE 10>>
 
 
: 10 : 
 
Accordingly, the Rule is discharged, however, without any order 
as to costs. 
Let a copy of this judgment and order be communicated to the 
respondents forthwith. 
 
Md. Mozibur Raman Miah, J.    
 
 
 
 
 I agree. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Mazhar, BO
input_summary: The PETITIONER, a defendant in a loan recovery suit, brought a writ against the RESPONDENTS challenging the money court's judgment and decree dated 23 September 2019 concerning secured credit liabilities. She sought a declaration that the decree lacked lawful authority. She argued that the decree improperly included mortgaged property, that no limitation issue was framed, and that the interest claim exceeded the statutory limit. The RESPONDENT argued that the PETITIONER had not used available remedies against the decree and had delayed bringing the writ. The parties referred to the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, the Code of Civil Procedure, the Limitation Act and Article 102 of the Constitution.
explanation: The court held that the Artha Rin Adalat Ain provides specific remedies against an ex parte decree and by appeal, neither of which the PETITIONER had used. It found no case of lack or excess of jurisdiction or fraud warranting writ intervention despite those remedies. The special statute prevails over inconsistent civil procedure provisions, and its provisions permit inclusion of mortgaged property in the execution schedule. The court considered the remaining objections, including the alleged interest error, matters for the appropriate statutory forum rather than writ adjudication.

                   IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BANGLADESH 
HIGH COURT DIVISION 
(Special Original Jurisdiction)

An Application under article 102 of the 
Constitution of the People’s Republic of 
Bangladesh.  
               And 
In the matter of: 
Prime Ship Recycling Limited and others         
                                                 … Petitioners 
              -Versus- 
The Learned Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka and 
another

Mr. Ehsan A. Siddiq, Senior Advocate with

Present:
