And 
Mr. Justice Rezaul Karim  
 
 
 
Md. Mozibur Rahman Miah, J. 
On an application under article 102 of the Constitution of the 
People’s Republic of Bangladesh, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the 
respondents to show cause as to why the order No. 13 dated 20.04.2025 
passed by the respondent No. 1 in Artha Rin Suit No. 1160 of 2024 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2 
(Annexure-A to the writ petition) allowing the applications for attachment 
before judgment of the property and shares of the petitioners should not be 
declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal 
effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court 
may seem fit and proper. 
At the time of issuance of the rule, the operation of the impugned 
order dated 20.04.2025 was stayed for a period of 04 (four) months which 
was subsequently extended from time to time.  
The salient facts leading to issuance of the rule are: 
The present respondent No. 2 as plaintiff originally filed the 
aforesaid suit claiming an amount of taka 134,35,67,642.19.  In the said 
suit, all the defendant nos. 1-3 filed a joint written statement denying the 
material averment so made in the plaint and ultimately prayed for dismissal 
of the suit. After that, the plaintiff, bank filed 2 application both on 
13.11.2024 under order 38 rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure prying for 
attachment of the landed property described in the schedule to the said  
applications one, with regard to the landed property and another one shares 
held by the defendant nos. 2 and 3. Against that application, the defendant 
nos. 1 and 2 also filed written objection denying all the material averment 
so made in the application for attachment before judgment and ultimately 
prayed for rejecting the same. Initially on the said application a show cause 
notice was issued upon the defendants and ultimately vide impugned 
judgment and order dated 20.04.2025 the court allowed the application of 
the plaintiff, bank. It is at that stage, the said defendant of the Artha Rin 
Suit came before this court and obtained instant rule and order of stay.  

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3 
Mr. Ehsan A. Siddiq, learned senior counsel along with Mr. Md. 
Mahbubur Rahman, learned counsel appearing for the petitioners upon taking us 
to the writ petition at the very outset submits that the provision provided in Order 
38 rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure has not at all been complied with in 
regard to disclose any definite information that the defendants were going to 
dispose of the property in the entire application file by the plaintiff and therefore 
the impugned order, cannot be sustained in law. To supplement the said 
submission, with reference to the impugned order the learned counsel also 
contends that nothing sort of any provision of Order 38, rule 5 has ever been 
discussed or observed which demonstrates, the impugned order bears any legal 
substance. The learned counsel by taking us to the application for attachment 
before judgment in particular paragraph no. 6 of two applications also contends 
that on the face of the alleged apprehension stated therein, it does not construe, 
the plaintiff gathered any definite information with regard to dispose of the 
landed property as well as the share scheduled in those 2 applications by the 
defendants in absence of which such vague application cannot be entertained  let 
alone allowing the same vide impugned order. The learned counsel by taking us 
to Annexure-‘C’ to the writ petition which is a deed of mortgage executed 
between the plaintiff as well as the defendants also contends that valuation of the 
proprieties has been fixed at taka 180 crore, so there has been no necessity on the 
part of the bank to file application for attachment if the valuation of the 
mortgaged property is taken into consideration. By taking us to the 
supplementary-affidavit filed today in particular, paragraph no. 10 to the same, 
the learned counsel also contends that it has been revealed from the ordering 
portion passed by the learned District Judge while disposing of a Miscellaneous 
Case filed for transfer  who clearly asserted that, the landed property as well as 
the shares of the defendant no. 2 has erroneously been shown  in the plaint which 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4 
has subsequently been strike out from the plaint and the case was then transferred 
to another Artha Rin Adalat which clearly indicates that the plaintiff bank from 
the very inception adopted ill practice in order to grab the personal landed 
property of the defendant no. 2 as well as his shares. In support of the assertion 
for not having any definite information with regard to transfer of shares, Mr. 
Ehsan A. Siddiq, referred a decision reported in 31 DLR (AD) 112 and takes us 
through paragraph no. 6 thereof where it has been held “The party imputing the 
motive on the defendant must be ready with the evidence to satisfy the court, if 
called upon to do so. Vague or general allegations without any material are 
insufficient to invoke the power of the court under this provision.” 
The learned counsel also referred another decision reported in 27 
DLR (HC) 256 and takes us through paragraph no. 11 where it has also 
been propounded that “The party must produce some definite materials 
before the court in order to satisfy it in this regard. Vague and general 
allegations can never be the foundation of the exercise of the extraordinary 
powers under the provision of Order XXXVIII, Rules 5 and 6 of the Code of 
Civil Procedure.” 
With those legal submissions, the learned counsel finally prays for 
making the rule absolute and set aside the impugned judgment and order.  
On the contrary, Mr. K.S. Salah Uddin Ahmed as well as Mr. 
Muhammed Mustafizur Rahman Khan, learned senior counsels appearing for the 
respondent, bank by filing affidavit-in-opposition very candidly opposes the 
contention taken by the learned counsel for the petitioners and at the very outset 
submits that the apprehension so have been expressed in paragraph no. 6 in both 
the application fled for attachment before judgment is sufficient to prove that the 
defendants were trying to dispose of their landed property as well as shares and 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5 
therefore the learned judge upon due consideration of that very material fact 
described by the bank in the application has passed the impugned order which is 
liable to be sustained.  
By taking us to Annexure-‘IV’ to the affidavit-in-opposition the learned 
counsel further contends that from the letter issued by a inspection company 
dated 21.09.2011 as well as another company dated 28.11.2022 it reveals that, 
the valuation of the property as described in the schedule to the plaint will not 
exceed taka 8,61,12,000/- so on that very cogent apprehension, the plaintiff, bank 
has rightly filed the application for attachment before judgment and if the 
property is not attached, the decreetal amount that might have passed against the 
defendants cannot be realized with selling the property mortgaged with the bank. 
When we pose a question to the learned counsel for the bank with regard to 
valuation so have been mentioned in mortgaged deed, the learned counsel then 
contends that, that very valuation does not imply the actual valuation of the 
landed property mortgaged at the time of obtaining loan and therefore basing on 
that valuation it cannot be said that the impugned order has been passed illegally. 
By adopting the submission so placed by the Mr. K.S. Salahuddin Ahmed, Mr. 
Khan another learned senior counsel also echoed the same view just added that 
since the apprehension has been found by the learned judge as of genuine one 
and the share has already been attached so there has been no scope to get any 
benefit by the defendants out of the said shares in the form of obtaining dividend 
out of those shares, so for that obvious reason, the shares have rightly been 
attached by the learned judge of the Artha Rin Adalat having no illegality in it. 
With the said submission, the learned counsel finally prays for discharging the 
rule.  

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6 
We have considered the submission so placed by the learned 
counsels for the petitioners and those of the learned senior counsels for the 
respondent no. 2, bank.  
Together, we have also very meticulously gone through the writ 
petition, all the document appended therewith vis-à-vis the affidavit-in-
opposition filed by the respondent no. 2 and that of the supplementary- 
affidavit filed by the petitioners today. Aside from that, we have also very 
carefully gone through the provision so have been provided in Order 38 
rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. On going through clause (a) and (b) 
of order 38 rule 5(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure we simply find, it has 
clearly been asserted therein that, the plaintiff bank has to gather a definite 
information with regard to dispose of the property which will  supposed to 
be attached by the bank. But on the plain reading of what has been asserted 
in the application for attachment for attaching the landed as well as the 
shares of the defendant nos. 1 and 2, we simply don’t find any reflection of 
that provision in the assertion made in the application rather in a very half-
hearted and slipshod manner, apprehension has been expressed and when 
we pose a question to the learned senior counsel, Mr. Muhammed 
Mustafizur Rahman Khan to that effect, he simply finds it difficult to go 
beyond to what has been stated in paragraph No. 6 of two application, Then 
if it is so, we are of the considered view that the above 2 clauses under 
Order 38 rule 5(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure has never been complied 
with by the plaintiff, bank. Furthermore, since in the mortgaged deed, the 
valuation of the landed property has clearly been mentioned at taka 180 
crore and on our query about the implication of mentioning that very 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7 
valuation, the learned senior counsel readily contends that said valuation 
had been evaluated only to realize the outstanding dues and if it is so, then 
the application for attachment before judgment is totally a futile exercise 
and a tool to harass the petitioners. Because, from the plaint we find that 
the claim has been made against the defendants for taka 134,35,67,642/19 
crore when the valuation of the mortgaged property has been set at 180 
crore which is way above the claim against the petitioners having no 
necessity on the part of the bank to file the application for attachment. So 
the submission placed by Mr. Ehsan A. Siddiq that from the very inception, 
the bank has been running after the defendants with an ill motive to grab 
the property and ultimately became successful by filing the application for 
attachment by including those properties which was earlier excluded by the 
learned District Judge while disposing a transfer Miscellaneous Case got 
substance.  
On top of that since the mandatory provision so have been provided 
in clause-(a) and (b) to Order 38 rule 5 has not been complied with as 
earlier found, so there had been no scope on the part of the trial court to 
pass such kind of frivolous impugned order and obviously we thus find 
substance in the decision cited by the learned counsel for the petitioners as 
reported in 27 DLR (HC) 256 and 31 DLR (AD) 112 to be squarely 
applicable in the case in hand. 
Regard being had to the above facts and circumstances, we don’t 
find any substance in the impugned judgment and order.   
Accordingly, the same is liable to be set aside.  

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8 
Consequently, the rule is made absolute however without any order 
as to costs. 
The impugned judgment and order dated 20.04.2025 passed by the 
respondent No. 1 in Artha Rin Suit No. 1160  of 2024 (Annexure-A to the 
writ petition)  is thus set aside.  
The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the rule is thus 
recalled and vacated.  
In view of the vacating the order of stay, there would have no 
necessity to pass any order on the application filed by National Credit and 
Commerce Bank PLC which was kept with the record vide order dated 
14.07.2026.  
 
Let a copy of this judgment and order be communicated to the 
respondents forthwith.    
 
Rezaul Karim, J.    
 
 
 
 
 I agree. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Kawsar/A.B.O.

They sought relief from the attachment, arguing that the applications gave no definite information that assets would be disposed of and that mortgaged property was valued above the claim. The RESPONDENT argued that its apprehension was sufficient and that other valuations showed the security might not cover the debt. Both sides relied on Order XXXVIII rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure; the petition invoked Article 102 of the Constitution.
explanation: The court found that the attachment applications expressed only a vague apprehension and did not supply definite information satisfying Order XXXVIII rule 5(1)(a) and (b) of the Code of Civil Procedure. It also noted that the mortgage deed valued the property at more than the amount claimed, and considered the additional attachment unnecessary on the record before it. The court applied authorities requiring concrete material rather than general allegations for this extraordinary measure and concluded that the trial court had not complied with the mandatory requirements.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BANGLADESH  
HIGH COURT DIVISION 
(CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION) 
 
Present: 
Mr. Justice Md. Bashir Ullah 
 
Criminal Appeal No. 6464 of 2024 
 
 
In the matter of: 
 
An Appeal under Section 10 of the Criminal 
Law Amendment Act, 1958. 
 
 
  
   And  
 
  
 In the matter of: 
 
 Nil Baran Tripura 
 
  
 
 
 
 
       ...Convict-Appellant 
                       -Versus- 
 
              
                    The State and another 
                                                                            ...Respondent 
 
Mr. Tapash Kumar Biswas with 
Mr. Pratikar Chakma, Advocates 
 
  
 
 
 
          ...For the Appellant 
 
                   Mr. S.M. Iqbal Bahar Bhuiyan, Advocate 
                                                        ...For the Respondent No.2 
 
     
 
Mr. Md. Mizanur Rahman, D.A.G and 
   
 
Mr. Md. Sirajul Karim, A.A.G  
                                                  … For the State 
 
 
 
     
Heard on: 18.06.2026, 14.07.2026 , 06.09.2026, 
and 09.09.2026 
 
  
Judgment on: 14.09.2026 
 
 
This appeal, preferred under Section 10 of the Criminal 
Law Amendment Act, 1958 is directed against the  judgment and 
order dated 30.03.2022 passed by the learned Special Judge, 
Sylhet in Special Case No. 12 of 2011 arising out of Chatak Police 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
Station Case No. 07 dated 14.04.2010 corresponding to G.R. No. 
87 of 2010 convicting the appellant under Section 161 of the 
Penal Code along with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of 
Corruption Act, 1947 and sentencing him to suffer rigorous 
imprisonment for 03 (three) years under Section 161 of the Penal 
Code and 03 (three) years under Section 5(2) of the Prevention of 
Corruption Act, 1947 with a fine of Taka 69,000/- in default to 
suffer imprisonment for 06(six) months as well. Both sentences 
were directed to run concurrently. 
  
The facts, relevant for disposal of the appeal, in short, are 
that one S.U.M. Ruhul Amin, Assistant Settlement Officer, 
Chatak, Sunamgonj lodged a First Information Report (FIR) 
against Nil Baran Tripura, the then Record Keeper with the 
Chatak Police Station, Sunamgonj, alleging inter alia that the 
informant had been serving as an Assistant Settlement Officer at 
the Upazila Chatak Settlement Office, Sunamgonj. The accused 
served as Record Keeper in the said settlement office from 
09.10.1991 to 15.09.2009 and thereafter upon his transfer served 
at the Bogura Zone Settlement Office. Based on allegations made 
by witnesses Nos. 1-8 in the FIR, the informant caused an inquiry 
to be conducted into the said allegations and upon completion 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
thereof submitted a report on 27.10.2009. Thereafter, based on the 
said inquiry report, the informant lodged the FIR alleging inter 
alia that during his tenure of service from 09.10.1991 to 
15.09.2009, the accused had forged the signature of the informant, 
issued purportedly false notices and used false appeal numbers 
and case receipts in respect of witness Nos. 1-8. The inquiry 
further disclosed that the said case numbers and notices had not 
been entered or registered in the relevant registers of the office. 
Witness No. 2 alleged that in 1998, the accused had received Taka 
9,000/- from him for the purpose of correction of the relevant 
record. Similar allegations were made by other witnesses that the 
accused had received money as illegal gratification by issuing 
false case receipts and notices. It was alleged that when the 
witnesses appeared before the office of the informant pursuant to 
such notices and case receipts, they came to learn that no 
corresponding entries existed in the official register of the office. 
The officers and witnesses allegedly came to suspect that the 
accused issued such false notices and case receipts in 
consideration 
of 
illegal 
gratification 
and 
had 
thereby 
misappropriated a huge amount of money. It was further revealed 
that the accused had issued many forged appeal case numbers by 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
forging the signatures of the concerned officers, including the 
informant during his tenure of service. The accused had tampered 
with many khatians (records) maintained in the settlement office 
by incorporating false names and false plot numbers therein. 
Furthermore, allegations were made that he had removed many 
case records and other official documents. In consequence of the 
aforesaid allegations, the informant lodged the case with the 
Chatak Police Station. Accordingly, Case No. 7 dated 14.04.2010 
was instituted under Sections 406/409/420/467/468 and 471 of the 
Penal Code, read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of 
Corruption Act, 1947. 
Thereafter, the police sent the said FIR to the Anti-
Corruption Commission, District Office, Sylhet for investigation, 
whereupon the investigating officer took up the investigation of 
the case. In the courses of investigation, the investigating officer 
seized certain documents from the office on 22.06.2010, 
23.06.2010 and 05.07.2010, respectively.  
On closure of the investigation and after obtaining the 
approval of the Anti-Corruption Commission, Md. Shamsul Alam, 
Assistant Director of the Anti Corruption Commission, Combined 
District Office, Sylhet submitted Charge Sheet No. 275 dated 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
28.12.2010 against the accused under Section 161 of the Penal 
Code read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 
1947. 
Subsequently, the case was transferred to the learned Senior 
Special Judge, Sunamgonj where it was registered as Special Case 
No. 12 of 2011. On 13.03.2011, the learned Senior Special Judge, 
Sunamgonj took cognizance of the offence. Subsequently, the 
learned Special Judge, Sunamgonj transmitted the case record to 
the learned Special Judge, Sylhet. Thereafter, the learned Special 
Judge, Sylhet framed charges against the accused under section 
161 of the Penal Code read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of 
Corruption Act, 1947 on 05.09.2012. The accused could not be 
examined as he remained absconding.  
 In the course of the trial, 13 prosecution witnesses were 
examined. The accused could not be examined under Section 342 
of the Code of Criminal Procedure as he remained absconding. 
 
Upon conclusion of the trial and hearing, the learned 
Special Judge, Sylhet convicted the accused under Section 161 of 
the Penal Code and Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption 
Act and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 03 (three) 
years under Section 161 of the Penal Code and to suffer rigorous 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
imprisonment for 03(three) years under Section 5(2) of the 
Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 along with a fine of Taka 
69,000/-. Both sentences were directed to run concurrently. 
 
Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and 
order of conviction and sentence, the convict-appellant preferred 
this Criminal Appeal before this Court.  
 
Mr. Tapash Kumar Biswas, learned Advocate appearing 
on behalf of the appellant contends that no witness established or 
proved that the accused received any bribe or illegal gratification.  
 
He further contends that the informant lodged the case 
against the accused merely to exculpate themselves. 
 
He further submits that PW 6 is the informant but failed to 
prove the First Information Report (FIR). In his testimony, he 
deposed a version distinct from and unsupported by the contents 
of the FIR. 
 
He next submits that there are material contradictions and 
inconsistencies in the evidence adduced by the prosecution 
witness. The accused served in the settlement office for more than 
20 years, during which period no allegations of illegal 
gratification were brought against him. The allegations were 
leveled only after his transfer. 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
 
He argues that the trial was conducted in absentia without 
proper issuance or service of summons or process upon the 
accused. 
 
He finally prays for allowing the appeal and for setting aside 
the judgment and order of conviction and sentence. 
 
 Per contra, Mr. S.M. Iqbal Bahar Bhuiyan, learned 
Advocate appearing on behalf of the Respondent No. 2, contends 
that the convict-appellant was a public servant and was not 
entitled to demand or receive any illegal gratification other than 
legal remuneration. 
 
He further contends that the prosecution witnesses proved 
that the accused by illegal means and by abusing his position as a 
public servant obtained pecuniary advantages. Thus, he committed 
offences punishable under Section 161 of the Penal Code and 5(2) 
of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. 
 
He next submits that the accused served in the Chatak 
Settlement Office, Sylhet from 09.10.1991 to 15.09.2009. It is 
alleged that in Chatak area BS survey commenced in 1996 and 
allegations were filed against the accused in 2007. So, it is not 
correct that the allegations were brought against the accused after 
his transfer. 

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8
 
He submits that the trial was lawfully conducted in absentia 
as he remained absconding which further demonstrates that the 
accused had a guilty mind. There is no procedural illegality or 
infirmity in the trial. Hence, the conviction and sentence ought to 
be sustained. Accordingly, he submits that the conviction and 
sentence imposed by the trial Court is lawful and proper and calls 
for no interference by this Court. Finally, he prays for the 
dismissal of the appeal.  
 
I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates 
for both sides, perused the impugned judgment and order passed 
by the trial Court and the materials on record. 
For proper adjudication of the appeal and to analyse the 
facts, the evidence of the prosecution witnesses is being reviewed 
below: 
PW 1, Md. Sad Ullah, Head Master of Bara Toka 
Government Primary School deposed that he instituted 3 appeals 
before the Chatak Settlement Office. The accused filled up the 
prescribed forms and collected money towards expenses. Nil 
Baran issued 3 receipts specifying appeal numbers. In fact, the 
appeals were never preferred or registered. He informed in writing 
to the Sylhet Zonal Office regarding the issuance of forged 

<<PAGE 9>>
 
9
numbers and submitted written allegations against the accused, 
Nil Baran Tripura. 
PW 2, Matiur Rahman deposed that he approached the 
accused for correction of his land record. The accused provided 
him with appeal documents and notices, all of which turned out to 
be false or fictitious. In fact, no appeal had been preferred. The 
accused received costs from him and subsequently, left without 
taking any official step. 
PW 3, Abul Kalam Azad deposed that the accused, Nil 
Baran received 40,000/- to Taka 45,000/- for filing an appeal. 
Subsequently, the accused became untraceable. Later, he learned 
that the higher authority lodged a case against the accused. 
PW 4, Md. Cherag Ali deposed that accused Nil Baran 
received a sum of money in connection with filing an appeal and 
issued a case number. Subsequently, the settlement office was 
destroyed by fire. Later, he learned that the higher authority 
lodged a case against the accused. 
PW 5, Md. Shamsul Alam, Investigating Officer deposed 
that he was entrusted with the investigation of the case. He 
recorded statements of the concerned witnesses under Section 161 
of the Code of Criminal Procedure and seized relevant documents. 

<<PAGE 10>>
 
10
Investigation revealed that the accused, Nil Baran Tripura 
accepted illegal gratification by issuing false case numbers, 
receipts, and notices during his tenure from 01.10.1991 to 
15.09.2009. Specifically, the accused received Taka 60,000/- from 
Abdul Matin Kachi Miah and Taka 9,000/- from Matiur Rahman. 
Thus, he committed offences punishable under Sections 
161/420/467/468/471 of the Penal Code read with Section 5(2) of 
the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He submitted the Charge 
Sheet upon obtaining the sanction from the Anti-Corruption 
Commission. He proved this sanction letter as Exhibit 9.    
PW 6, S.U.M. Ruhul Amin, the informant deposed that he 
served as Assistant Settlement Officer before 14.04.2010. The 
accused served as Record Keeper in his office from 09.10.1991 to 
15.09.2009. During his service, he received illegal gratification 
from various persons to file appeals. He issued forged case 
numbers and receipts. Upon instruction from higher authorities, 
PW 6 lodged the case against the accused who had also forged his 
signature.  
He proved the FIR as Exhibit 10.  
PW 7, S.M. Mozzemel Haque deposed that he served as 
Deputy Assistant Settlement Officer before 04.07.2010. The 

<<PAGE 11>>
 
11
accused served as Record Keeper from 09.10.1991 to 15.09.2009 
during which time he accepted illegal gratification and issued 
fictitious case numbers and receipts. He also forged the signature 
of the Assistant Settlement Officer. The Assistant Settlement 
Officer subsequently lodged the case against the accused. 
PW 8, Md. Abul Khair deposed that he served as Peshkar-
in- Charge. He is a seizure list witness. He proved the seizure lists 
as Exhibits 2, 7 and 8. 
He deposed that the accused received illegal gratification 
from numerous individuals. 
PW 9, Md. Delwar Hossain deposed that the Investigating 
Officer seized certain documents. He proved the seizure list as 
Exhibit 7 and Jimmanama as Exhibit 8. 
PW 10, Md. Abdus Sattar deposed that he served as 
Surveyor. The Investigating Officer seized certain documents 
from Peshkar Abul Khayer in his presence. 
He proved the seizure list as Exhibit 7 and Jimmanama as 
Exhibit 8. 
PW 11, Md. Sana Ullah and PW 12, Md. Soleman were 
tendered by the prosecution. 

<<PAGE 12>>
 
12
PW 13, Md. Abdul Mannan deposed that on 05.07.2010, the 
investigating officer seized a few documents and placed him under 
his custody. He proved the documents as Material Exhibit V. 
 
Upon evaluation of the evidence of PW 1, (Md. Sad Ullah) it 
appears that he failed to state whether he personally paid any bribe 
and the quantum of money paid to the accused. Even, he failed to 
state the date time or place of such payment or filing of the appeal. 
Thus, his evidence lacks specific, actionable allegations against 
the accused. The evidence may raise suspicion regarding the 
regularity of the transactions, but it falls short of establishing, with 
the requisite degree of certainty, the demand or acceptance of 
illegal gratification by the appellant.  
 
Upon scrutiny of the evidence adduced by PW 2, Matiur 
Rahman, it appears that he failed to specify any exact sum 
allegedly received by the accused. Although the FIR mentions that 
the accused-appellant took Taka 9,000/-, but this assertion has not 
been substantiated through oral evidence. PW 2 failed to mention 
the date, time and place of the alleged payment of Taka 9,000/-. 
The mere presence of an allegation in the FIR cannot take the 
place of substantive evidence in establishing the fact alleged. 

<<PAGE 13>>
 
13
 
Similarly, the contents of the FIR are not corroborated by the 
testimony of PW 3, namely Abul Kalam Azad who failed to state 
the date, time and place of the alleged transaction. He deposed in 
his examination-in-chief that “Bp¡j£ e£m hle Bj¡l L¡R −b−L 40/45 
q¡S¡l V¡L¡ ®eu 31 d¡l¡u Bf£m Ll¡l SeÉz flha£Ñ−a Bp¡j£−L Bl f¡Ju¡ k¡u 
e¡Cz flha£Ñ−a ö¢e Bp¡j£l EàÑae A¢gp¡l a¡l ¢hl¦−Ü  j¡jm¡ L¢lu¡−Rz” 
 
It appears from the above-mentioned evidence that the 
witness did not state the precise amount allegedly paid. The date 
and time of alleged receipt of money was not stated. No other 
prosecution witness has corroborated the material allegation. The 
FIR also does not contain any specific allegation regarding receipt 
of money by the appellant from the said Abul Kalam Azad (PW3). 
Such 
material omission 
assumes 
significance 
when the 
prosecution seeks to establish a specific act of acceptance of 
illegal gratification. 
 
PW4 likewise failed to depose as to the specific sum 
allegedly paid to the accused and no prior complaint had been 
lodged by him before any competent authority regarding the 
alleged demand or acceptance of an illegal gratification. Thus, his 
evidence also does not furnish sufficiently specific proof of the 
essential element of acceptance of illegal gratification. 

<<PAGE 14>>
 
14
 
The Investigating Officer (PW5) deposed that the accused 
received Taka 60,000/- from one Abdul Mukit Kachi Miah but he 
was not examined as a prosecution witness. However, in this 
regard, nothing was stated in the First Information Report. 
Moreover, no other prosecution witness corroborated that the 
accused took illegal gratification from Abdul Mukit Kachi Miah. 
No satisfactory explanation has been offered for withholding this 
material witness, particularly when the Investigating Officer relied 
upon the alleged payment of Taka 60,000/- as an incriminating 
circumstance against the appellant. 
The evidence of the Investigating Officer as to what he 
learnt during investigation cannot, by itself, proves the fact of 
payment of alleged illegal gratification by the appellant. Such 
evidence, insofar as it merely reproduces information allegedly 
received from an unexamined person, cannot constitute 
substantive proof of the alleged transaction. 
 
It is thus apparent from an overall assessment of the 
prosecution evidence that the allegations regarding illegal 
gratification remain substantially uncertain and uncorroborated. 
The prosecution witnesses have not consistently specified the 

<<PAGE 15>>
 
15
amount allegedly paid, the date and place of such payment, the 
circumstances in which the demand was made, or the particular 
official act for which the gratification was allegedly demanded or 
accepted. The evidence regarding forged notices, fictitious case 
numbers and irregularities in official records may create a degree 
of suspicion against the appellant, but suspicion, however grave, 
cannot take the place of proof beyond reasonable doubt. 
It is also significant that the prosecution case itself 
attributes several acts to the appellant extending over a 
considerable period of time. Yet the evidence led at trial does not 
satisfactorily connect any particular alleged receipt of illegal 
gratification with a particular official act performed or intended to 
be performed by the appellant. The prosecution was required to 
establish the charge by reliable and legally admissible evidence 
and not merely by the cumulative effect of allegations, official 
irregularities and suspicion. 
 
The trial Court, in convicting the appellant, appears to have 
attached considerable significance to the allegation that the 
appellant remained absconding during the trial. Such conduct, 
however, cannot independently furnish a safe basis for conviction. 

<<PAGE 16>>
 
16
 
The record indicates that the appellant had joined in the 
Settlement Office on 14.11.1988. He had served at the Chatak 
Settlement Office from 09.10.1991 to 15.09.2009. Thereafter, he 
had been transferred to Zonal Settlement Office, Bogura, when he 
joined on 18.10.2009. He served there until 24.12.2021, when he 
retired from service. Meanwhile, the informant lodged the FIR 
against the accused-appellant on 14.04.2010. It is the specific case 
of the appellant that neither the Investigating Officer nor the 
concerned office took effective steps to secure his presence from 
his known place of employment or residence. 
The record, as placed before me, does not demonstrate that 
any warrant of arrest was executed upon him at his place of 
service or that such effective process was served upon him there. 
There is also no material showing that proclamation under Section 
87 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or the consequential 
proceeding contemplated under Section 88 thereof was duly 
undertaken against him. 
In such circumstances, the mere fact that the appellant was 
not present during the trial cannot, without proof that he had 
knowledge of the proceeding and deliberately evaded it, be 

<<PAGE 17>>
 
17
converted into an incriminating circumstance. Absence from trial 
and conscious evasion of the process of law are not synonymous. 
The surrounding circumstances must establish that the accused 
was aware of the proceeding and intentionally avoided the process 
of the Court before any adverse inference can safely be drawn 
from such conduct. 
The subsequent conduct of the appellant also assumes 
relevance. According to the materials on record, he came to know 
about the judgment on 05.09.2023, thereafter he surrendered 
before the trial Court on 03.10.2023 and subsequently preferred 
the present appeal. Such conduct is not wholly consistent with an 
inference that he had deliberately remained beyond the reach of 
law with knowledge of the pending trial. In any event, even if his 
absence during trial is taken into consideration, such circumstance 
cannot cure the fundamental deficiency in the substantive 
evidence relating to the alleged demand and acceptance of illegal 
gratification. 
 
In this regard, reliance may be placed upon the decision 
passed in the case of State Vs. Lalu Miah and another, reported 
in 39 DLR(AD)(1987)117 wherein it has been held that: 

<<PAGE 18>>
 
18
‘Absconsion 
by 
itself 
is 
not 
an 
incriminating 
matter, 
for, 
even 
an 
innocent person, if implicated in the 
ejahar for a serious crime, sometimes 
absconds to avoid harassment during 
investigation by the police.” 
 
The significance of abscondence, therefore, depends upon 
the facts and circumstances of each particular case. 
 
Similarly, in the case of State Vs. Balai Chandra Sarker, 
reported in 47 DLR(1995)467 wherein it has been held that: 
“... abscondance cannot be presumption or 
inference of guilt without any supporting 
evidence or conclusive circumstance. 
From the conduct of a person for 
absconding after commission of the 
offence may sometimes be evidence to 
show that he was concerned with the 
offence. But it is usually a very small item 
in the evidence on which a conviction can 
be based.” 

<<PAGE 19>>
 
19
The prosecution must first establish substantive evidence 
connecting the accused with the offence.  
It is also material that the prosecution has not produced the 
person from whom the alleged payment of Taka 60,000/- was said 
to have been received by the appellant, while the alleged payment 
of Taka 9,000/- attributed to PW2 has not been proved with the 
requisite specificity. The alleged payment of Taka 40,000/- to 
Taka 45,000/- spoken to by PW3 is likewise uncertain as to the 
precise amount, date, time and place of payment and remains 
uncorroborated. These deficiencies are not merely peripheral 
discrepancies; they go to the root of the prosecution case 
concerning the essential ingredient of acceptance of illegal 
gratification. 
It is a settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that where 
two views are reasonably possible on the evidence, the view 
favourable to the accused must prevail. More importantly, before a 
person can be convicted, the prosecution must establish the charge 
beyond reasonable doubt by legally admissible, reliable and 
convincing evidence. The Court cannot sustain a conviction 

<<PAGE 20>>
 
20
merely because the conduct of the accused appears suspicious or 
because certain irregularities are established in the official records. 
Upon a careful and anxious consideration of the entire 
evidence on record, I find that the prosecution has failed to prove 
beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant demanded or accepted 
illegal gratification as alleged. The evidence regarding the alleged 
payments is vague, inconsistent, uncorroborated or based upon 
information not proved through the persons concerned. The 
evidence concerning forged notices, fictitious case numbers and 
irregularities in the official records, even if accepted, does not by 
itself establish the charge under Section 161 of the Penal Code 
read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. 
 
In view of the foregoing discussion, I am of the considered 
opinion that the trial Court failed to appreciate the evidence in its 
proper perspective and that the conviction is not founded upon 
evidence of such quality as would satisfy the standard of proof 
required in a criminal case and the judgment and thus the order of 
conviction and sentence cannot be sustained in law and is liable to 
be set aside. 

<<PAGE 21>>
 
21
 
I find merit in the appeal and substance in the submission 
advanced by the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the 
appellant. 
 
In the result, the appeal is allowed. 
 
The judgment and order dated 30.03.2022 passed by the 
learned Special Judge, Sylhet in Special Case No. 12 of 2011 
arising out of Chatak Police Station Case No. 7 dated 14.04.2010 
corresponding to G.R. No. 87 of 2010 is hereby set aside. 
 
The appellant is acquitted of the charge levelled against him. 
 
The convict-appellant is released from his bail bond.  
 
Let the judgment along with the Lower Court Records 
(LCR) be communicated to the Court concerned forthwith.  
 
         
                   (Md. Bashir Ullah, J.) 
 
 
 
 
Md. Ariful Islam Khan 
Bench Officer
input_summary: The APPELLANT, a former public record keeper, challenged the special judge's judgment dated 30 March 2022 concerning convictions and sentences for alleged illegal gratification. The appeal was brought against the STATE and a RESPONDENT. The prosecution alleged that the APPELLANT took money for land-record appeals and issued fictitious notices and case numbers. The APPELLANT sought relief from the convictions, arguing that payments were unproved, witness accounts conflicted, and the trial proceeded in his absence without proper process. The RESPONDENT argued that the witnesses established abuse of public office and that the absence was deliberate. The parties referred to the Penal Code and the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947.
explanation: UNCERTAIN: The court assessed the Penal Code and Prevention of Corruption Act charges together on the same evidentiary grounds, without identifying a single decisive statute. It found that alleged payments lacked reliable particulars or corroboration and that a material alleged payer was not examined. Official irregularities and fictitious notices raised suspicion but did not establish the demand or acceptance of illegal gratification beyond reasonable doubt. The court also found no adequate proof that the APPELLANT knowingly evaded trial process; absence alone could not supply the missing substantive evidence.

<<PAGE 1>>
 
 
Present: 
Mr. Justice Md. Salim 
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.120 OF 2024 
Md. Rashel Uddin  
              ...................Appellant. 
-Versus- 
The State and another  
            ...............Respondent. 
 
Mr. Al Reza Md. Amir, Advocate 
...........For the Appellant.

Mr. Syed Akhtarul Islam, AAG

Heard on 26.07.2026 and 27.07.2026  
Judgment on: 03.08.2026 
This appeal is directed against the judgment and order of 
conviction and sentence dated 15.11.2023 passed by the learned 
Judge, Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal No.1, Cox’s 
Bazar, in Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Case No.12 of 2020, 
convicting the appellant under section 11(ga) of Nari-O-Shishu 
Nirjatan Daman Ain, 2000 (Amendment- 2003), and sentencing 
him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 2(two) years with a fine 
of Tk.20,000/- in default to suffer simple imprisonment for 4 
(four) months more.  
The prosecution case, in brief, is that P.W.1, Esmot Ara 
Begum brought a complaint before the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan 

<<PAGE 2>>
-2- 
 
 
Daman Tribunal, Cox’s Bazar, against the convict-appellant 
alleging, inter alia, that the complainant was married to the 
accused-appellant on 23.02.2016 in accordance with Muslim 
Shariah. After the marriage, the accused-appellant demanded 
dowry from the complainant on several occasions. Lastly, on 
04.08.2019 at about 6:00 p.m., the accused-appellant again 
demanded Tk.1,00,000/- for his business from the complainant 
and, upon her refusal to meet the said demand, subjected her to 
severe physical torture.   
Upon receipt of the complaint petition, the learned Judge 
of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal No. 1, Cox’s 
Bazar, examined the complainant under Section 200 of the Code 
of Criminal Procedure and took cognizance of the offense 
against the convict appellant under Section 11(ga) of the Nari-O-
Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, and, thereafter, directed the Deputy 
Director, Women Affairs Department, Cox’s Bazar, to conduct 
an inquiry into the allegations. Pursuant to the said direction, the 
concerned officer conducted the inquiry and submitted his report 
on 09.09.2019. 
The learned Judge of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman 
Tribunal, Cox’s Bazar, framed the charge against the appellant 
under Section 11(ga) of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 

<<PAGE 3>>
-3- 
 
 
2000 (Amendment- 2003), which was read over and explained to 
him, who then pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. 
During the trial, the prosecution examined 06 (six) 
witnesses, while the defense examined none. 
After the evidence was closed, this appellant was not 
examined under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 
due to his absence from the court. 
Subsequently, the learned Judge, Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan 
Daman Tribunal No.1, Cox’s Bazar, by the judgment and order 
dated 15.11.2023, found the appellant guilty under Section 
11(ga) of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 2000, and 
sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 2 (two) years 
with a fine of Tk.20,000/- in default, to suffer simple 
imprisonment for 4 (four) months more. 
Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the above 
judgment and order of conviction and sentence, the accused 
appellant preferred the instant appeal. 
Mr. Ali Reza Md. Amir, the learned Counsel appearing on 
behalf of the appellant, taking us through the impugned 
judgment, evidence, and other materials on record, submits that 
the learned Judge of the Tribunal failed to consider the defense 
case at all, overlooking the fact that the witnesses have not 

<<PAGE 4>>
-4- 
 
 
corroborated the allegation against the appellant; the prosecution 
failed to prove the cause of the victim’s injury by adducing a 
valid injury certificate; the doctor, having issued the incorrect 
injury certificate, committed professional misconduct; that the 
learned Judge of the Tribunal has failed to consider that, save 
and except the P.W.1-victim, all the witnesses are hearsay 
witnesses who have contradicted each other. Therefore, the 
appellant is liable to be discharged from the charge levelled 
against him. 
On the contrary, Mr. Monzurul Alam Sujan, the learned 
Deputy Attorney General for the State, opposes the contention so 
made by the learned advocate for the appellant and submits that 
the prosecution successfully proved the charge against the 
appellant by adducing and producing the oral and material 
evidence. He then submits that the learned Judge of the Nari-O-
Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal has perfectly and justifiedly 
convicted and sentenced the appellant based on the most cogent 
and reliable evidence. 
We have heard the learned advocate for the appellant and 
the learned Deputy Attorney General for the State, and have 
gone through the impugned judgment, the evidence, and other 
materials on record.  

<<PAGE 5>>
-5- 
 
 
In order to prove the charge, the prosecution examined as 
many as 06 (six) witnesses. Of them, P.W.1, Ismat Ara Begum, 
in her deposition, stated that the accused is her husband. She 
stated that on 04.08.2019 at about 6:00 p.m., while she was at her 
rented residence at Kamal Mansion, Baitush Sharaf Mosque 
Road, the accused demanded Tk.1,00,000/- from her for his 
business. As she failed to provide the said amount, she was 
assaulted by the accused with a wooden stick in the presence of 
the witnesses, causing injuries to her right shoulder and back. At 
that time, Ramiza, Bazal Ahmed, and Faridul Alam were present, 
and the accused restrained them. Thereafter, the witnesses took 
her to Sadar Hospital, and the case was instituted. The petition of 
complaint was produced and marked as Exhibit-1, and her 
signature thereon was marked as Exhibit-1/1 and 1/2. 
P.W.-2, Ramiza Begum, in her deposition, stated that the 
complainant is her younger sister and the accused is her sister’s 
husband. It was stated that the occurrence took place on 
04.08.2019 at about 6:00 p.m. at the rented residence of the 
complainant at Kamal Mansion, Baitush Sharaf Mosque Road, 
Cox’s Bazar. At about 4:00 p.m., the complainant telephoned her 
and informed her that her husband had assaulted her. Upon 
receiving the information, she went to the place of occurrence, 

<<PAGE 6>>
-6- 
 
 
and the other two witnesses arrived shortly thereafter. Upon 
arrival, the complainant was found sitting on the bed, while the 
accused was found in another room. Thereafter, the accused 
came out and assaulted the complainant with a wooden stick 
measuring approximately one and a half hands in length, and 
blows were inflicted upon her waist and back. She restrained the 
accused. According to her deposition, the complainant was 
assaulted as she had failed to provide Tk.1,00,000/- demanded by 
the accused for the purpose of his business. Thereafter, the 
complainant was again assaulted in the presence of the other two 
witnesses, who also intervened and restrained the accused. 
Subsequently, the complainant was taken to the Sadar Hospital. 
P.W.-3, Bazal Ahmed, in his deposition, stated that the 
complainant is his niece. It was stated that the occurrence took 
place on 04.08.2019 at about 6:00 p.m., after Maghrib, at a 
rented residence on Baitush Sharaf Road. At about 3:30 p.m., he 
received a telephone call from the complainant, Ismat, 
whereupon he proceeded towards the place of occurrence by 
CNG. On the way, Ramiza and Farid also joined them. 
Thereafter, they went to the complainant’s residence, where the 
complainant and the accused were found sitting beside each 
other on chairs in the same room. In their presence, the accused 

<<PAGE 7>>
-7- 
 
 
demanded Tk.1,00,000/- from the complainant for his business. 
When the complainant expressed her inability to provide the said 
amount, she was immediately assaulted by the accused with a 
wooden stick. Although the witnesses intervened and attempted 
to restrain the accused, the assault was continued. Thereafter, the 
complainant was taken to Sadar Hospital for treatment, and she 
subsequently instituted the case.  
P.W.-4, Monowara Begum, in her deposition, stated that 
the occurrence took place on 04.08.2019 at about 6:00 p.m. It 
was stated that the accused, Rashed Uddin, demanded 
Tk.1,00,000/- as dowry from the complainant, Ismat Ara. When 
the complainant expressed her inability to provide the said 
amount, she was assaulted and injured by the accused with a 
wooden stick in her presence. Thereafter, other witnesses arrived 
at the place of occurrence, and the complainant was rescued and 
taken to the hospital by them. 
P.W.-5, Dr. Mizanur Rahman, in his deposition, stated that 
Ismat Ara was examined by him on 04.08.2019 for medical 
treatment. Upon examination, a swelling injury was found on her 
left shoulder. The medical certificate was produced and marked 
as Exhibit-2, and his signature thereon was identified and marked 
as Exhibit-2/1.  

<<PAGE 8>>
-8- 
 
 
P.W.-6, Md. Kalu, in his deposition, stated that on 
04.08.2019 at about 6:00 p.m., upon hearing the cries of Ismat 
Ara, he went to the place of occurrence and asked the accused, 
Rashed, why Ismat Ara was being assaulted. In reply, Rashed 
stated that Tk.1,00,000/- was required from Ismat Ara for his 
business. When Ismat Ara stated that she had no money and 
asked from where she would arrange the said amount, she was 
assaulted by Rashed with a wooden stick. Thereafter, Ismat Ara 
was rescued and taken to the hospital. 
Analyzing the above evidence on record, it appears that, in 
the petition of complaint, the complainant alleged that on 
04.08.2019 at about 6:00 p.m., the accused-appellant demanded 
Tk. 1,00,000/- from her for his business and, upon her refusal to 
comply with the said demand, she was assaulted by him with a 
wooden stick. P.W.1, the complainant, in her deposition, stated 
that the accused-appellant demanded Tk.1,00,000/- from her for 
his business; similarly, P.W.3 – P.W. 6 stated that the accused 
demanded Tk.1,00,000/- from the complainant for his business.  
Section 2() of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain 
provides that money, articles, or any property demanded by the 
bridegroom or his father, mother, or anybody directly related to 

<<PAGE 9>>
-9- 
 
 
the bridegroom party as a condition for consideration of marriage 
is called dowry. 
In the instant case, having evaluated the evidence on 
record, it appears that the convict appellant demanded 
Tk.1,00,000/- for business purpose from his wife (complainant); 
therefore we are of the firm view that the prosecution failed to 
prove that the convict appellant demanded money as dowry at 
the relevant time of the occurrence. Therefore, the alleged 
demand of money of Tk. 1,00,000/- does not fall within the 
purview of the definition of dowry contemplated in section 2( ) 
of the Ain. 
Further, it appears that upon refusal to provide the said 
demand, the complainant-victim was assaulted by the convict 
appellant with a wooden stick, causing injuries to her right 
shoulder and back. In that regard, P.W.1, the complainant, stated 
that she had sustained an injury on her right shoulder. P.W. 2 
stated that the convict appellant inflicted injuries to the victim’s 
waist and back; P.W. 3, 4 and 6 did not mention the point of 
injuries of the victim. On the contrary, P.W. 5, the doctor who 
examined the victim, stated that upon examination, a swelling 
injury was found on her left shoulder. Moreover, Exhibit 2, the 

<<PAGE 10>>
-10- 
 
 
medical certificate, also shows that a swelling injury was present 
on the left shoulder. Therefore, a discrepancy exists between the 
complainant’s oral evidence between the evidence of P.W.5 the 
doctor and the medical certificate regarding the location of the 
alleged injury, which creates a serious doubt about the allegation 
of physical torture of the victim by the convict appellant which 
cast a serious doubt as to the alleged occurrence and the 
prosecution case.  
In view of the above facts and circumstances, it appears 
that the learned Judge of the Tribunal failed to evaluate the 
evidence on record properly to establish that the implication of 
the convict-appellant in the felony has been established by 
credible, reliable, and clinching evidence. The prosecution left 
no stone unturned to rope in the convict-appellant and overdid its 
job by fabricating false evidence and a colored version. 
Therefore, the learned Trial Judge committed a serious error in 
presuming the guilt of the convict-appellant first and, thereafter, 
attempting to find another reason to justify such a conclusion 
without an objective, independent, and impartial analysis of the 
materials before recording a finding of guilt against the convict-
appellant. The doubtful and suspect nature of the evidence 

<<PAGE 11>>
-11- 
 
 
sought to be relied upon to substantiate the circumstances 
suffered from serious infirmities and lacked legal credibility. 
Accordingly, the findings of the learned Judge of the tribunal do 
not deserve the merit of approval of this Court, having regard to 
the infirmities and illegalities vitiating the judgment and the 
patent errors apparent on the face of the record, resulting in a 
serious and great miscarriage of Justice in convicting the 
appellant.  
In view of the above facts and circumstances, we are of the 
firm view that the prosecution failed to prove the charge under 
section 11(ga) of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Dama Ain against 
the convict appellant; thus, we held that the prosecution case is a 
hoax, having no ground under its legs. So, the impugned 
judgment is liable to be set aside. 
Resultantly, the appeal is allowed.  
The judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 
15.11.2023 passed by the learned Judge, Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan 
Daman Tribunal No.1, Cox’s Bazar, in Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan 
Case No.12 of 2020, arising out of C.P Case No. 386 of 2019, is 
hereby set aside. 

<<PAGE 12>>
-12- 
 
 
The accused-appellant is acquitted of the charge leveled 
against him and discharged from his bail bonds.  
Send down the lower Court records with a copy of this 
judgment. 
 
........................ 
(Md. Salim, J). 
 
 
 
Rakib(ABO)
input_summary: The APPELLANT challenged the tribunal's judgment dated 15 November 2023 concerning a conviction and sentence for alleged dowry-related violence against the STATE and a RESPONDENT. The RESPONDENT, his spouse and complainant, alleged that he demanded money for business and assaulted her when she did not provide it. The APPELLANT sought relief from the conviction, arguing that witnesses gave inconsistent or second-hand accounts and that the injury evidence was unreliable. The STATE argued that oral and medical evidence established the charge. The proceedings concerned section 11(ga) of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 2000, as amended in 2003.
explanation: The court applied the statutory definition of dowry and found that the evidence described a demand for business funds rather than a demand established as consideration for marriage. It also identified a discrepancy between the complainant's account of injury to her right shoulder and the medical evidence of swelling on the left shoulder; other witnesses described different or unspecified locations. The court considered these discrepancies significant to the alleged assault and found the evidence insufficient to prove the charge reliably beyond reasonable doubt.

arrears of maintenance due to the opposite party and the 
minor daughter, in accordance with law. If the petitioner 
demonstrates genuine financial hardship before the Executing 
Court, that Court may, in the exercise of its discretion and on 
such just and equitable terms as it considers appropriate, 
allow payment of the decretal amount by instalments. Any 
such arrangement shall preserve the decree-holder's rights 
and interest. 
The order of stay granted earlier is recalled. 
 
The office is directed to send down the Subordinate 
Court's Record (SCR) with a copy of this judgment and order, 
forthwith.         
The Court appreciates the learned counsel's diligent 
submissions and assistance in resolving the issues. 
Order accordingly. 
 
( Abdur Rahman, J)

He sought a fresh hearing, arguing that he had not received summons, had paid part of the dower, and should be able to produce evidence. He also cited financial hardship and requested an opportunity to pay in instalments. explanation: The court found that the lower courts had concurrently accepted the evidence establishing the marriage, divorce, dower and maintenance obligations, and saw no legal or jurisdictional error requiring intervention. It left the executing court discretion to consider instalments if genuine hardship is demonstrated, while preserving the decree-holder's rights.

input_summary: The REVISIONISTS, defendants in a land partition suit, challenged the appellate court's judgment dated 11 September 2022 concerning the OPPOSITE PARTIES' claimed inherited shares and an earlier decree. They sought relief from the lower courts' decisions, arguing that inheritance was unproved and that land records and rent receipts supported their own claim through purchase. The OPPOSITE PARTIES asserted that they inherited from a recorded tenant, had not been included in the earlier suit, and that the alleged transfer by their predecessor was unsupported by a deed. The application invoked revisional jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure; the reported submissions identified no other statute.
explanation: The court found that the OPPOSITE PARTIES' predecessor was a recorded owner and that the REVISIONISTS did not prove their alleged purchase from her. A defence witness admitted that no deed from her had been proved and that her heirs were omitted from the earlier suit. The court accepted the concurrent findings that the OPPOSITE PARTIES inherited shares and were necessary parties to that proceeding. It found no material misreading or perversity in the lower courts' assessment of the evidence.

were given promotion to the post of Laboratory Technician from 1994 
and after wards. 
The post of Laboratory Technicians were created respectively in

official gazette on 30.04.1995 amended the Local Government 
Engineering Bureau (Officers and Staff) Recruitment Rules, 1986 by 
providing provision for appointment of Laboratory Technician in serial

the power conferred under Article 133 read with Article 142(2) of the 
Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh framed Rules, 
namely, Local Government Engineering Department (Officers and Staffs) 
Recruitment Rules, 2009 keeping the provision for appointment of 
Laboratory Technician in serial No. 30 only from the Science Graduates

Graduation Degree have been discharging their functions as Laboratory

upgraded as 2nd class gazetted officer keeping the petitioners who are

have been doing the same nature of job, the petitioners have been placed

petitioners being Science Graduates discharging same functions as 
Laboratory Technicians as 3rd Class employees.

We have taken into account that pursuant to the judgment passed in

They sought an upgraded gazetted status with retrospective effect and changes to promotion provisions in the 2009 recruitment rules. They argued that technicians with science degrees performed the same work as diploma holders but had lower status, and that their rules provided no route to higher posts. explanation: UNCERTAIN: The court applied recruitment rules rather than a named Act, and its final order did not expressly determine every requested remedy. It found the PETITIONERS similarly situated to technicians whose posts had been upgraded after an earlier writ and noted that the RESPONDENTS did not oppose comparable treatment. Because the PETITIONERS were appointed before 2009, the court considered their promotion governed by the 1986 rules, subject to the requisite conditions. It directed an upgrade of their posts, but did not expressly order retrospective effect or invalidate the 2009 rules.

input_summary: The PETITIONER challenged the appellate tribunal's judgment dated 1 February 2021 concerning release of land from the vested property list in proceedings against the STATE and a RESPONDENT. The PETITIONER sought relief from that judgment and claimed title through a registered purchase, arguing that it preceded the RESPONDENT's deed and that he was omitted from an earlier specific-performance suit. The RESPONDENT relied on an earlier sale agreement and a later court-executed deed, disputed the PETITIONER's deed, and asserted possession. The STATE opposed the writ. The petition invoked Article 102 of the Constitution; the judgment also recounts the STATE's reliance on legislation governing enemy and vested property.
explanation: UNCERTAIN: The final order preserved possession and deferred release to the eventual title holder, but did not expressly resolve the requested challenge or release the property to the PETITIONER. The court found that both private parties claimed through the same predecessor, that the validity of the PETITIONER's deed was disputed, and that proceedings affecting the RESPONDENT's decree remained pending. Those competing title questions could not be resolved in summary writ proceedings. The court therefore required title to be determined by the competent civil forum before release to either claimant.

previous Regulations;

question is whether such subsequent regulation may be applied

accrued under the earlier regulation.

referred by the counsel of the petitioner.

Amin Munshi and another, 21 BLC (AD) 85 wherein it has been held

to Article 133 of the Constitution which affects the vested 
rights of a person or contravenes independent 
constitutional provisions or violates fundamental rights

Constitution. Moreover, retrospectivity will be arbitrary 
and unconstitutional if the date from which retrospective 
effect is given has no reasonable nexus with the 
provisions contained in the amending rules. In other

time but not to the detriment to the rights or privileges 
that existed at the relevant time when an employee of 
such appointing authority entered into it's service."

Noor and others, 66 DLR(AD)187, i has been held as under: 
"The appointing authority enjoys the power and the 
authority to frame new rules to regulate the service of its 
employees, but in no way, can take away the 
accrued/vested rights of its employees." 
In the case of Bangladesh Bank Vs. Sukamal Sinha, 21 BLC

or disadvantage to the privilege that existed at the 
relevant time when an employee of such appointing 
authority entered into its service."

Nuruzzaman and others, 24 BLT(AD)171 it has been held as under: 
"There is no dispute that the petitioner got appointment

that is, he is entitled to get the benefits as provided in 
Service Rules of 1988 and his service would be regulated

rightly held that the provisions of Service Rules of 2005 
are to be effective in respect of the appointment of the 
employees who have been appointed on 21.01.2005 or

Further there is long lines of the decision of our apex Court 
that without declaring any provision of the law to be ultra vires the 
Constitution, this Court has power to give the substantive relief as 
prayed for, the Appellate Division in the case of Dr. Nurul Islam Vs. 
Bangladesh, 33 DLR (AD) 201 has held that where the substantive 
relief claimed in the writ petition can be granted without striking 
down any legal provision, that course is to be followed. In the said 
case, the then Hon'ble Chief Justice Mr. Justice Kemaluddin Hossain 
observed as follows: 
"I like to adhere to the well established self-set rule 
which says, the Court will not declare a law 
unconstitutional, if the case in which the question is 
raised can be properly disposed of in some other way." 
So, it is clear that the Court has ample power to give the 
substantive relief as claimed in the writ petition without striking 
down the legal provision challenged in the writ petition to be ultra 
vires the Constitution.

considered for promotion prescribed by the 2011 Regulations before

consideration for promotion had, therefore, accrued under the 
previous regulation. 
The mere repeal of the 2011 Regulations does not, by itself, 
authorize the respondents to retrospectively extinguish such accrued 
eligibility. 
Accordingly, we hold that the newly framed promotion 
regulation, 2021 cannot be applied retrospectively to the petitioners 
who had already become eligible for promotion prior to the 
amendment. The petitioners possess vested rights that accrued under 
the previous regulation of 2011 and these rights cannot be taken 
away by subsequent changes in regulation. Accordingly, the 
petitioners who had fulfilled the required service criteria, 
qualifications and other conditions before the enforcement of the 
amended regulation, 2021 shall be considered for promotion strictly 
in accordance with the old regulation, 2011. Any new condition 
introduced later shall not adversely affect their accrued eligibility.  
For the reasons stated above, we find substance in the Rule. 
Accordingly, the Rule Nisi is disposed of with the following 
directions: 
The respondents are directed to consider the petitioners, insofar 
as they had already fulfilled the prescribed eligibility requirements

lawful requirements relating to suitability and promotion within a 
period of 01 (one) month in accordance with law. 
The ad-interim order of direction stands disposed of in 
accordance with this judgment.

Resultantly, the Rule Nisi is disposed of with above direction. 
No order as to costs.

They sought relief from the new provisions and consideration for promotion under the earlier regulations. They argued that they had completed the qualifying service before 2021, that reducing promotion opportunities impaired accrued eligibility, and that different treatment from other engineering categories was discriminatory. The RESPONDENT argued that the authority could amend regulations, that the earlier rules had ceased to apply, and that length of service did not guarantee promotion. The parties relied on the 2011 and 2021 employee service regulations.
explanation: UNCERTAIN: The court relied on service regulations rather than a named Act, and granted consideration under the old rules without invalidating the challenged provisions. It found that the PETITIONERS had completed the qualifying service under the 2011 regulations before the 2021 changes. Their accrued eligibility for consideration could not be extinguished retrospectively, although the authority could amend rules prospectively. The court distinguished an opportunity to be considered from an entitlement to promotion and made consideration subject to vacancies, suitability and other lawful requirements.

From reading the above provisions it is crystal clear 
that the delinquent is entitle to get a notice of show 
cause regarding the allegation and if after completion of 
departmental proceeding the delinquent is found guilty and 
authority concerned decided to impose penalty/penalties 
then the delinquent is entitled to get another notice 
regarding the proposed penalty. This opportunity of being 
heard is the principle of natural justice which is 

<<PAGE 14>>
 
14
ingrained in the legal systems of all civilized nations. It 
has been also settled by a catena of decisions from the 
Higher Courts of this subcontinent that without following 
the principle of natural justice, no action can be taken 
against anyone. In the case of Ridge Vs. Baldwin 1964 AC 40 
Mr. Ridge was dismissed as chief constable by the watch 
committee under the relevant provisions of law which 
provides ‘the watch committee may at any time dismiss, any 
borough constable whom they think negligent in the 
discharge of his duty, or otherwise unfit for the same’ and 
this dismissal was affirmed by the Home Secretary. Lord 
Reid in the House of Lords, held: the power of dismissal in 
the Act of 1882 could not then have been exercised and 
cannot now be exercised until the watch committee have 
informed the constable of the grounds on which they propose 
to proceed and have given him a proper opportunity to 
present his case in defence. Our Supreme Court in the case 
of Bangladesh Small Industries Corporation Vs. Mahbub 
Hossain reported in 29 DLR (SC) 41 upheld that decision and 
observed: 
(a) 
If an employee is dismissed or his service 
is 
terminated 
in 
contravention 
of 
a 
mandatory statutory provision, the employee 
has a right of action either in a superior 
Court in its writ jurisdiction or a Civil 
Court. 
(b) 
If the service of its employee is terminated 
in violation of the principle of natural 
justice, the employee has a similar right of 
action as in (a).  
(c) 
If the office is a statutory one, the holder 
of the office has similar right of action as 
in (a) in case of termination of the said 
office not in accordance with the law, under 
which the said office has been created. 

<<PAGE 15>>
 
15
(d) 
In spite of the office  being a statutory 
one or of public character, terms and 
conditions of the office may be regulated by 
contract, and termination of service in 
contravention 
of 
such 
contract, 
but 
otherwise than in the manner mentioned in 
(a) and (b) is not actionable for the 
purpose of reinstatement in the office. 
(e) 
Terms and conditions of service prescribed 
by rules, regulations or any other form of 
delegated legislation made by a body under 
statutory powers are not contractual, but 
have statutory force and the dismissal or 
termination 
of 
service 
in 
substantial 
disregard of them will entitle the employee 
to a right of action as in (a).          
In that case our apex Court further observed that an 
employee of a statutory Corporation of public character, 
who does not hold any statutory post or status can 
nevertheless maintain an action in a Court of law, on a 
limited ground, that of violation of any mandatory 
statutory provision as to the kind of contract or the 
statutory ground of dismissal, or on the doctrine of ultra 
vires or the violation of the rule of natural justice. In 
the case reported in 56 DLR (AD) 24 it is held that even 
where provisions for show cause notice and opportunity of 
personal hearing are not available, the principle of 
natural justice shall be applied unless it is specifically 
barred. Similar view has been taken in the case reported in 
65 DLR (AD) 243.   
It is true that there is some exception in applying 
this principle of natural justice: if the appointment is 
void ab initio or the appointment is obtained by practicing 
fraud or by submitting false document or the appointee had 
no eligibility to be appointed in the post, then in a very 

<<PAGE 16>>
 
16
exceptional case the authority can take action against him 
if it is so urgent that if a show cause notice is served 
then the purpose may be frustrated. Even in that case, the 
Indian Supreme Court and our Supreme Court held that the 
delinquent is entitled to get an opportunity after the 
action has been taken. In the case reported in (2005) 7 SCC 
764 the Indian Supreme Court took a view that dismissal 
without show cause may be permissible where exigencies of 
situation require that prompt action and not taking prompt 
action might result in the trouble spreading and situation 
worsening and at times becoming uncontrollable. In the case 
reported in AIR 2000 SC 2783 the Indian Supreme Court 
observed that the absence of a notice to show cause does 
not make any difference for the employee has already been 
told that if his further overstay is for continuing in the 
job with foreign University, it is bound to be refused. The 
case of the delinquent thus falls, on the admitted or 
indisputable facts, only one view is possible. In that 
event no prejudice can be said to have been caused to the 
delinquent though notice has not been issued. Thus in 
India, the Supreme Court has distinguished between: A 
voidable or irregular appointment (e.g, some procedural 
defect, but the person was otherwise eligible). A void or 
non est appointment (e.g, appointment obtained by clear 
fraud or forged documents). In the first case principle of 
natural justice applied while in the latter case (such as 
the person never possessed a mandatory qualification and 
the authority had no jurisdiction to relax it, or the 
appointment 
was 
secured 
by 
proven 
forgery), 
courts 
sometimes say that no enforceable right ever accrued and 
the person can be removed without full departmental 
proceedings, but even then many decisions insist on at 
least a minimal hearing to verify the facts before branding 
the appointment ‘void’. Our Supreme Court, both High Court 
Division and Appellate Division, has taken firm view that 

<<PAGE 17>>
 
17
removal on the ground of illegal or irregular appointment 
will normally attract the principle of natural justice 
which is the general rule and only when the appointment is 
a clear nullity in law, and statute or Constitution itself 
dispenses with hearing, can the authority justify omitting 
a prior opportunity of being heard.                 
Now, in the settled principle as stated above let us 
consider the present case. In the present case we have 
already noticed that the plaintiff claimed that there was 
an advertisement for appointment which has not been denied 
by the defendants and the plaintiff was appointed in a post 
called ‘Chowkidar’. The prevailing law provides the name of 
the 
post 
as 
‘Mahalladar’ 
though 
previously 
it 
was 
‘Chowkidar’. The plaintiff had no hand in the appointment 
letter whether it is written Moholladar or Chowkidar. For 
all practical purpose this post is known as Chowkidar to 
everyone from pre-partition period to even today. Hence, it 
comes under the doctrine of factum valet quod fiery non 
debuit (what ought not to be done becomes valid once done). 
In other words, the deed is valid though it ought not to 
have been done. The doctrine stands for the principle that 
where a fact is accomplished, i.e where an act is done and 
finally accomplished, though it may be in contraventions of 
texts, the fact will stand and the act will be deemed to be 
legal and binding provided there is no fraud, coercion, or 
violation of mandatory provision. The idea that once a 
certain act has been completed and accepted, minor 
irregularities or procedural defects in how it was done 
will not automatically render it invalid and undoing it 
would cause greater harm or injustice, the law may treat it 
as valid. In the present case the appointment letter of the 
plaintiff should have been issued in the name of the post 
as Mahalladar but the authority mentioned it as Chowkidar 
and for that reason it cannot be said that the plaintiff 
was appointed in a non est or non-existent post. It appears 

<<PAGE 18>>
 
18
from the resolution dated 29.11.2007, though it was not 
served upon the plaintiff-petitioner, that the Union 
Parishad under the Chairmanship of the defendant No.2 took 
a resolution that the plaintiff indulged himself in 
unethical activities and liable for negligence in his duty. 
These are serious nature of allegations and stigma against 
the plaintiff and the authority was bound to issue show 
cause notice upon the plaintiff as per his service law, i.e 
The Union Council (Village Police Force) Rules, 1968 to 
explain his position.  
From going through the service rules applicable for 
the plaintiff-petitioner as mentioned above it is crystal 
clear and admitted position that the procedure for taking 
action against the plaintiff has not been followed by the 
authority on the plea that the appointment of the plaintiff 
petitioner by the defendant no.3 was not legal as by order 
of stay the defendant no.2 resumed his office of Chairman 
and the defendant no.3 was not Chairman-in-charge. It is 
surprising that the defendant No.2 claimed that he resumed 
office on 14.03.2005 but the plaintiff who was appointed on 
19.03.2005 continued his service till August, 2008 and drew 
his government portion of salaries till July, 2008 and 
after resuming his office the defendant No.2 or the 
defendant No.1 did not feel that the appointment of the 
plaintiff was illegal and did not take any action but long 
after more than 03(three) years all of a sudden the 
defendant No.2 decided that the appointment of the 
plaintiff was illegal which create serious doubt and it 
cannot be ruled out that the act of the defendant nos.1 and 
2 was done malafide. On the other hand as per claim of the 
defendant no.14 (the present opposite party no.1), he was 
appointed in the post on 03.12.2008 and joined on 
04.12.2008, clearly during pendency of the suit and as such 
there was 
no 
requirement of 
law to challenge 
his 
appointment as an consequential relief by the plaintiff-

<<PAGE 19>>
 
19
petitioner in the present suit. The suit was maintainable 
in its present form. I have already observed that the 
procedure as mentioned above has not been followed hence 
the dismissal order and the impugned notice was illegally 
issued upon the plaintiff. As such the plaintiff is 
entitled to get the decree as prayed for. Both the 
judgments and decrees passed by the courts below are liable 
to be set aside as such I have no option but to interfere 
with the impugned judgments and decrees passed by the 
courts below.   
In the result the Rule is made absolute. There will be 
no order as to cost.   
Accordingly, the impugned judgment and decree dated 
10.07.2024 (decree drawn on 16.07.2024) passed by the Joint 
District Judge, 3rd Court, Naogaon in Title Appeal No. 09 of 
2024 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the 
judgment and decree dated 05.10.2023 (decree drawn on 
10.10.2023) passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Naogaon 
in Other Class Suit No. 230 of 2008 dismissing the suit is 
hereby set aside and the impugned order passed by the 
defendants is declared illegal and not binding upon the 
plaintiff. The plaintiff is entitled to get full relief and 
as such the suit is decreed accordingly. The authority 
concerned is directed to reinstate the plaintiff in his 
post with all his arrear salaries.                           
Send down the lower court records along with this 
judgment at once.    
  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Ziaul Karim 
Bench Officer
input_summary: The REVISIONIST, a former village police employee, challenged the appellate court's judgment dated 10 July 2024 concerning his removal from service by the OPPOSITE PARTIES. He sought reinstatement and arrear salary, arguing that he had worked and received pay for years but was removed on allegations of misconduct without notice or a hearing. The OPPOSITE PARTY contended that the appointment was unlawful, the removal followed a council resolution, and the suit lacked a necessary challenge to a replacement appointment. The parties referred to the Union Council (Village Police Force) Rules, 1968 and the Specific Relief Act, as well as the Code of Civil Procedure.
explanation: UNCERTAIN: The decisive named instrument is a set of service rules rather than an Act. The court found that the REVISIONIST had served and drawn salary for years and that the different name used for the post did not make the appointment nonexistent. The misconduct allegations required the notices and hearing prescribed by rule 9(10), which were not provided. The court also found the suit maintainable without a challenge to the replacement's appointment, because that appointment occurred after the suit began. It found the removal inconsistent with the service rules and natural justice.
